While self-reflection provides internal error correction, it cannot fully replace human oversight for several reasons. Agents can overweight feedback from other agents who are themselves mistaken, creating reinforcing error loops. Agents lack the specialized intuition and contextual judgment that humans bring. And agents can get stuck in repetitive reasoning patterns or dead ends that require external intervention to break. Human-in-the-loop integration provides three critical functions: course correction when the agent commits to a wrong path, alignment assurance to ensure outputs match human expectations, and dead-end recovery when the agent becomes trapped in unproductive reasoning loops. Human oversight is not a limitation on agent capability but a safeguard that ensures the agent's reasoning remains grounded in reality.

Key Points

  • Agents tend to commit prematurely to reasoning paths, and errors compound through subsequent steps.
  • Self-reflection cannot fully replace human oversight because agents can reinforce each other's mistakes.
  • Human feedback provides course correction, expectation alignment, and dead-end recovery.
  • Without human oversight, inter-agent error reinforcement can escalate, driving the system further from correct solutions.
  • Human-in-the-loop is a safeguard for reality alignment, not a constraint on agent capability.
1
Agent Commits to Path
The agent selects a reasoning direction and begins executing; errors at this stage are not yet visible
2
Error Compounding
If the initial direction is wrong, each subsequent reasoning step amplifies the deviation from the correct solution
3
Human Review Point
A human evaluates the agent's intermediate output, applying domain expertise and contextual judgment
4
Course Correction
The human provides feedback or redirection, realigning the agent's reasoning with the intended outcome
5
Improved Output
The agent incorporates human feedback and produces a result aligned with reality and expectations
💡 Math Error Cascade
A wrong initial assumption in a multi-step calculation propagates through every subsequent step, making the entire solution incorrect despite correct intermediate procedures.
💡 Reasoning Dead End
An agent loops through the same ineffective approach repeatedly; a human redirects it to a productive alternative strategy.
Key Takeaways
  • Always include human checkpoints at critical decision points in agent workflows.
  • Treat human-in-the-loop as a design principle, not an optional add-on.

Section 20: Governance and Safety

5 lectures

▼

Lesson 99: Governance Patterns

Governance patterns are the guardrail mechanisms that ensure agents operate safely and ethically, forming a critical layer on top of workflow, memory, and feedback patterns.

Core Concept

Agent architecture progresses through several foundational layers: workflow patterns make agents productive, memory and feedback patterns make agents intelligent, and governance patterns ensure agents remain safe and ethical. Governance is the guardrail layer that constrains agent behavior within acceptable boundaries, preventing harmful, biased, or non-compliant actions. This layer is not optional; it is a critical component of modern AI agent architecture that deserves deliberate design attention equal to the productivity and intelligence layers.

Key Points

  • Governance patterns sit atop workflow, memory, and feedback layers as the safety and ethics layer.
  • They constrain agent behavior within acceptable boundaries to prevent harmful outcomes.
  • Governance is not optional; it is architecturally mandatory for production systems.
  • This layer ensures agents operate in alignment with organizational and societal standards.
Key Takeaways
  • Treat governance as a first-class architectural layer, not a compliance afterthought.
  • Every production agent system requires explicit governance mechanisms.

Lesson 100: Guardrails and Policy Enforcement

Agent safety is achieved through three layered mechanisms: input guardrails (filtering harmful data before it reaches the agent), output guardrails (screening agent responses before they reach users), and policy enforcement (system-prompt rules using positive and negative prompting to constrain behavior).

Core Concept

Just as road safety depends on multiple layered mechanisms (guardrails, speed limits, traffic lights, road signs) rather than any single measure, AI agent safety requires a combination of specialized protective layers. No single mechanism provides sufficient protection; the system's resilience comes from the interplay of multiple defenses. Three distinct safety mechanism types protect agent systems. Input guardrails filter the data an agent receives, operating on the principle that avoiding exposure to harmful content reduces the likelihood of harmful behavior. Output guardrails screen the agent's responses before they reach end users, catching hallucinations, unsafe content, and non-compliant responses. Policy enforcement communicates complex behavioral rules through the system prompt, typically combining positive prompting (what the agent should do) and negative prompting (what it must avoid). Together, these three layers create a defense-in-depth strategy where a failure in one layer is caught by another.

Key Points

  • No single safety mechanism is sufficient; layered defenses are required.
  • Input guardrails prevent harmful or inappropriate data from reaching the agent.
  • Output guardrails screen agent responses for hallucinations, unsafe content, and compliance violations.
  • Policy enforcement uses system-prompt rules (positive and negative prompting) to constrain agent behavior.
  • The three layers create defense-in-depth: if one fails, others provide backup protection.

Input Guardrails

Filter incoming data to prevent the agent from being exposed to harmful, biased, or inappropriate content

Output Guardrails

Screen agent responses before delivery, catching hallucinations, unsafe content, and policy violations

Policy Enforcement

System-prompt rules using positive and negative prompting to define acceptable and prohibited behaviors

Defense-in-Depth

Multiple overlapping safety layers ensure that a failure in one mechanism is caught by another

💡 Road Safety Analogy
Guardrails, speed limits, traffic lights, and road signs each address different risk vectors; combined, they create comprehensive safety.
💡 Content Screening
An agent generates a response that contains an unsupported medical claim; the output guardrail detects and removes it before delivery to the user.
Key Takeaways
  • Implement all three guardrail types; relying on a single layer leaves critical gaps.
  • Combine positive prompting (desired behaviors) with negative prompting (prohibited behaviors) for robust policy enforcement.

Lesson 101: Cost Limiter

A cost limiter is a governance mechanism that caps an agent's resource consumption (tokens, dollars, or API calls) to prevent runaway costs from loops, excessive queries, or unexpected behavior, triggering graceful shutdown and human escalation when the budget is exhausted.

Core Concept

Traditional software has relatively predictable cost profiles: development, deployment, and maintenance expenses can be estimated with reasonable certainty. AI agents operate fundamentally differently. They run continuously, make thousands of LLM and API calls daily, and can behave unpredictably, getting stuck in loops, over-querying APIs, or generating unexpectedly expensive outputs. This makes cost forecasting difficult and creates a significant business risk. The cost limiter addresses this by establishing hard boundaries on agent resource consumption. Limits can be defined in terms of tokens consumed, dollar amounts spent, or number of API calls made. When the agent reaches its predefined budget, it shuts down gracefully and delivers a fallback response, informing the user it cannot continue. In customer-facing scenarios, the agent can escalate the interaction to a human operator who takes over the conversation. The cost limiter functions as a governance mechanism that provides financial predictability while preventing runaway consumption.

Key Points

  • AI agents have inherently unpredictable cost profiles compared to traditional software.
  • Agents can incur excessive costs through loops, over-querying, or generating expensive outputs.
  • Cost limiters cap consumption using tokens, dollars, or API call counts.
  • When limits are reached, the agent shuts down gracefully with a fallback response.
  • Human escalation provides continuity when cost limits terminate an agent mid-interaction.

Token Limits

Cap the total number of tokens consumed across prompts and responses within a defined period

Dollar Limits

Set a monetary ceiling on total API and compute costs per session, day, or month

API Call Limits

Restrict the number of external API invocations to prevent over-querying and runaway costs

Graceful Shutdown

When any limit is reached, the agent stops processing, delivers a helpful fallback, and optionally escalates to a human

💡 Customer Service Cost Cap
A support agent hits its token budget during a complex conversation and gracefully hands off to a human operator with full conversation context.
💡 Loop Prevention
An agent stuck in a retry loop is automatically stopped by the cost limiter before it exhausts the daily API budget.
Key Takeaways
  • Every production agent must have a cost limiter; unbounded agents are a financial liability.
  • Design the graceful shutdown experience so users receive a helpful handoff, not an abrupt failure.

Lesson 102: A/B Shadow Testing

A/B shadow testing evaluates a new agent version by running it invisibly alongside the production version on real user traffic, logging its outputs for comparison without ever exposing users to the untested version, thereby eliminating risk to the customer experience.

Core Concept

Updating a production AI agent is not an exact science. New versions do not always guarantee better performance, and rolling out an unproven update risks degrading the experience of real customers. A/B shadow testing provides a zero-risk evaluation method. The technique works by maintaining two concurrent versions: the original production version (A) that all users continue to interact with, and the new version (B) that runs in a shadow environment. The shadow version receives the same user inputs and context as the production version but its outputs remain hidden from users. Instead, these outputs are logged and compared against version A's responses across multiple dimensions: latency, accuracy, governance compliance, and overall user experience quality. This approach allows engineers to observe how changes perform under real traffic conditions, with authentic user prompts and context, without any risk to the actual customer experience. Once analysis confirms the new version is reliable across all evaluation dimensions, it can be gradually rolled out to production users through a controlled deployment process.

Key Points

  • The production version (A) remains the only version users interact with; the new version (B) runs invisibly in shadow mode.
  • Shadow version processes real user inputs but its outputs are logged, never displayed to users.
  • Comparison dimensions include latency, accuracy, governance compliance, and user experience quality.
  • This eliminates all risk to the customer experience during evaluation.
  • Positive shadow results enable a controlled, gradual rollout to production.
1
Deploy Shadow Version
Launch the new agent version (B) in a background environment alongside the live production version (A)
2
Mirror Real Traffic
Route identical user inputs and context to both versions simultaneously
3
Log Shadow Outputs
Capture version B's responses without displaying them to users; users only see version A
4
Comparative Analysis
Evaluate version B against version A on latency, accuracy, compliance, and quality metrics
5
Controlled Rollout
If shadow results are positive, gradually shift real user traffic to the new version
💡 Customer Support Agent Update
A revised support agent runs in shadow mode alongside the production version for two weeks, processing identical queries; logs reveal it is 15% more accurate with similar latency, supporting a gradual rollout.
Key Takeaways
  • Use A/B shadow testing before any production agent update to eliminate customer risk.
  • Evaluate shadow results across multiple dimensions; accuracy alone is insufficient.

Lesson 103: Bias and Fairness Systems

Bias concerns are amplified in agent systems because, unlike LLMs that only produce text for human evaluation, agents can take autonomous actions that create real-world consequences; mitigations must span the entire system (LLM, tools, memory, planning, inter-agent communication), not just the model layer.

Core Concept

The critical difference between LLMs and agents in the context of bias is agency. When an LLM produces biased text, a human can still read, evaluate, and choose whether to act on it. When an agent exhibits bias, it can autonomously take actions that produce real-world consequences before any human review occurs. This makes even minor reasoning biases in agents potentially consequential. Furthermore, placing an LLM within an agentic framework multiplies the points where bias can emerge. Beyond the model itself, bias can enter through external data sources, memory systems, planning mechanisms, tool interactions, and inter-agent communication. The entire system, not just the LLM, must be audited for fairness. Mitigation strategies operate at multiple levels. Human oversight at various stages of the agent lifecycle provides expert evaluation of ethical and professional compliance. Prompt engineering at the model level uses positive and negative rules to prevent problematic outputs. The agent's decision-making layer can serve as an external, hard-coded safety net that enforces fairness rules even when the LLM itself fails to comply. The complexity of multi-step, multi-tool agent workflows makes bias detection more challenging, but the stakes make it essential.

Key Points

  • Agents amplify bias risk because they can act autonomously, creating real-world consequences without human review.
  • Bias can enter at any point: LLM, data sources, memory, planning, tools, and inter-agent communication.
  • The entire agentic system must be audited for fairness, not just the underlying model.
  • Human oversight, prompt engineering, and hard-coded decision-layer rules form a multi-level mitigation strategy.
  • Multi-step agent workflows make bias harder to detect but more important to address.

Agent Action Amplification

Unlike text-only LLMs, agents can act on biases autonomously, creating real-world consequences

Multi-Point Bias Entry

Bias can emerge from LLM training, data sources, memory, planning, tools, or inter-agent communication

Human Oversight Layer

Human review at lifecycle stages ensures compliance with ethical and professional standards

Hard-Coded Decision Rules

External fairness rules in the decision-making layer enforce constraints even when the LLM fails to self-regulate

💡 LLM vs. Agent Bias Impact
A biased LLM generates questionable text that a human can evaluate; a biased agent autonomously acts on that same bias, potentially affecting real users before anyone reviews the action.
💡 System-Wide Bias Entry Points
Bias enters through a training dataset, is amplified by a biased memory retrieval, and compounds through planning steps before manifesting in an automated action.
Key Takeaways
  • Audit the entire agent system for bias, not just the LLM; every component is a potential bias entry point.
  • Implement hard-coded fairness rules in the decision layer as a safety net independent of LLM compliance.

Section 21: Evaluation and Benchmarking

4 lectures

▼

Lesson 104: Section Introduction

Agent evaluation is a continuous process, not a one-time event; performance must be monitored and improved throughout the agent's lifecycle using both offline benchmarks and online metrics.

Core Concept

Launching an AI agent is not the finish line. Without ongoing performance monitoring and improvement, the agent cannot serve as a reliably helpful tool. Evaluation must be planned alongside the agent itself, not treated as an afterthought. This final module defines how to measure agent performance using offline benchmarks (controlled testing with curated datasets) and online metrics (real-time monitoring in production), and addresses the key challenges inherent in evaluating autonomous agent systems.

Key Points

  • Agent evaluation is continuous, spanning the entire lifecycle from development through production.
  • Both offline benchmarks and online metrics are needed for comprehensive evaluation.
  • Evaluation planning should occur during the design phase, not after deployment.
  • Autonomous agent systems present unique evaluation challenges beyond traditional software testing.
Key Takeaways
  • Plan evaluation strategy during agent design, not as a post-launch activity.
  • Use both offline benchmarks and online metrics for comprehensive coverage.

Lesson 105: How to Measure Agent Performance

Agent performance is measured across five interconnected dimensions (accuracy, cost, latency, safety, and user experience), with the primary KPI varying by use case and improvements in one dimension almost always coming at the expense of another.

Core Concept

Evaluating an AI agent requires balancing multiple performance dimensions simultaneously, much like judging a car by speed, fuel efficiency, safety, reliability, and comfort rather than any single metric. The five critical dimensions are accuracy, cost, latency, safety, and user experience. These dimensions are deeply interconnected and involve inherent tradeoffs. Increasing accuracy may require larger models that increase latency and cost. Optimizing for speed may sacrifice thoroughness. A perfectly reliable system is useless if it is not safe for end users. Beyond a certain level of optimization, improvements in one area almost always degrade another. The primary KPI (North Star metric) varies by use case. A trading agent prioritizes accuracy above all else. An agent serving high-value clients focuses on user satisfaction and experience. A high-volume, low-revenue customer service agent must maximize cost efficiency. There is no universal ranking of these metrics; the specific use case determines which dimension takes priority while the others serve as constraints.

Key Points

  • Five critical dimensions: accuracy, cost, latency, safety, and user experience.
  • These dimensions are interconnected; improving one typically comes at the expense of another.
  • The North Star metric varies by use case: accuracy for trading, satisfaction for high-value clients, cost for high-volume services.
  • No universal metric ranking exists; the use case determines priority.
  • Performance measurement must be defined on a case-by-case basis, not with a one-size-fits-all framework.
5
Core performance dimensions: accuracy, cost, latency, safety, user experience
1
North Star metric selected per use case as the primary optimization target
4
Remaining dimensions serve as constraints, not ignored, but secondary to the North Star
N
Tradeoff combinations increase with system complexity; evaluate interactions, not metrics in isolation
💡 Trading Agent
Accuracy is the top priority; the cost of a wrong prediction far exceeds any latency or compute savings.
💡 High-Volume Service Agent
Cost efficiency is paramount; the agent must handle thousands of low-revenue interactions within tight budget constraints.
💡 High-Value Client Agent
User satisfaction and experience quality are the North Star; clients expect premium, personalized interactions.
Key Takeaways
  • Identify the North Star metric for the specific use case before designing the evaluation framework.
  • Always evaluate how optimizing the primary metric affects the other four dimensions.

Lesson 106: Offline Benchmarks

Offline benchmarks evaluate an agent against curated, labeled datasets under controlled conditions before deployment, estimating success rates (accuracy, error rate) without risking real user experiences, though their effectiveness depends entirely on the quality and currency of the test data.

Core Concept

Offline evaluation measures an agent's performance in controlled conditions using curated datasets and predefined scenarios, without exposing real users to the untested system. The agent processes a set of labeled inputs (e.g., 500 past support tickets with known correct responses) and its outputs are compared against the gold-standard labels to calculate metrics such as accuracy and error rate. This approach mirrors A/B shadow testing in its risk-free philosophy but operates on historical data rather than live traffic. Several tools automate the process, including LangChain Evals and HELM. The primary advantage is zero risk to existing users. The primary limitation is that historical data may not accurately represent current business conditions, user behaviors, or edge cases. The effectiveness of offline benchmarks is therefore directly tied to the quality, relevance, and recency of the sample data. Offline benchmarks are typically deployed during the middle-to-late development phase, before production launch. They serve as a guiding framework that highlights areas requiring optimization and provides confidence (or reveals gaps) before the agent encounters real-world unpredictability.

Key Points

  • Testing occurs on labeled, historical datasets under controlled conditions, not with real users.
  • Agent outputs are compared against gold-standard labels to calculate accuracy and error rates.
  • Tools like LangChain Evals and HELM automate the offline evaluation process.
  • Zero risk to existing users is the primary advantage.
  • Effectiveness depends on the quality, relevance, and recency of the test dataset.
  • Best used in the middle-to-late development phase as a pre-deployment quality gate.
Aspect Offline Benchmarks Online Metrics
Data Source Curated historical datasets with labels Real-time production traffic
User Risk Zero; no real users are exposed Present; real users interact with the agent
Data Currency May be outdated or unrepresentative Current and authentic
When Used Pre-deployment (development phase) Post-deployment (production phase)
Key Advantage Risk-free quality estimation Authentic, real-world performance measurement
Key Limitation Historical data may not match current conditions Requires careful monitoring to protect user experience
Tools LangChain Evals, HELM Custom dashboards, logging frameworks
💡 Support Ticket Benchmark
A customer support agent is tested on 500 past tickets with known correct responses; outputs are compared to the gold standard to estimate production-readiness.
Key Takeaways
  • Use offline benchmarks as a pre-deployment quality gate, but do not assume they fully predict production performance.
  • Invest in curating high-quality, representative test datasets; benchmark quality directly determines evaluation quality.

Lesson 107: Online Metrics

Online metrics evaluate agent performance in production through real user interactions, tracking task success rate, latency, interaction duration, user satisfaction, and business KPIs as an interconnected system of indicators that must be interpreted holistically, like medical diagnostics.

Core Concept

When an agent is deployed in production, no amount of offline testing can fully replicate the unpredictability of real-world user interactions. Online metrics provide the real-time performance signal by tracking how the agent performs across thousands of live interactions. Five standard online metrics form the evaluation framework. Task success rate measures how often users achieve their intended goal. Agent latency tracks response times. Interaction length measures session duration from start to completion. User satisfaction is gauged through surveys, UX tests, and repeat usage patterns. Business KPIs connect agent performance to commercial outcomes such as sales, subscriptions, renewals, and churn rates. Critically, these indicators must be interpreted as parts of an interconnected system, analogous to how doctors interpret blood test results. A single metric reveals only one aspect; only by examining all indicators together can the full picture of agent health be understood. A high task success rate means little if latency is unacceptable, and excellent user satisfaction is unsustainable if the cost per interaction exceeds revenue.

Key Points

  • Online metrics measure real production performance through live user interactions.
  • Five standard metrics: task success rate, agent latency, interaction length, user satisfaction, and business KPIs.
  • No single metric provides a complete picture; all must be interpreted as an interconnected system.
  • Business KPIs connect agent performance to commercial value (sales, subscriptions, churn).
  • Online metrics are essential when no historical data exists for offline benchmarking (e.g., new products).
TSR
Task Success Rate: percentage of interactions where the user achieves their intended goal
Latency
Agent Latency: average response time from query to result delivery
Duration
Interaction Length: time from session start to successful task completion
CSAT
User Satisfaction: measured via surveys, UX tests, and repeat visit patterns
KPIs
Business KPIs: sales, subscriptions, renewals, churn, and revenue impact metrics
💡 Real Estate App Agent (Aerocom)
A startup with no historical data deploys a property-search agent live, tracking task success rate, latency, interaction duration, user satisfaction surveys, and KPIs like property sales, premium subscriptions, and churn rate.
Key Takeaways
  • Interpret online metrics holistically as an interconnected system, not as isolated data points.
  • Always connect agent performance metrics to business KPIs to demonstrate commercial value.

Section 22: Introduction to LangChain

4 lectures

▼

Lesson 108: Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) process and generate human-like text; LangChain is a Python framework that orchestrates LLM-powered applications by abstracting away the complexity of prompt management, memory, retrieval, and agent tooling.

Core Concept

Large Language Models are deep learning models trained on massive text corpora that can understand statistical relationships between tokens and generate coherent, human-like responses. The term 'large' is relative and continues to scale: GPT-2 (2019) had 1.5 billion parameters trained on 40 GB of text, GPT-3 (2020) jumped to 175 billion parameters trained on 570 GB of data (approximately 400 billion tokens), and GPT-4 pushed the boundary further still. LangChain is a Python library designed to simplify the development of applications powered by these models. Rather than writing low-level API calls and managing prompts, memory, and data pipelines manually, LangChain provides modular, composable abstractions that handle each concern. It integrates with multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others), making it possible to swap underlying models without rewriting application logic.

Key Points

  • LLMs learn statistical relationships between tokens to predict the most likely next token in a sequence, enabling text generation
  • Model scale has grown exponentially: GPT-2 (1.5B params) to GPT-3 (175B params) to GPT-4 (undisclosed but significantly larger)
  • LangChain abstracts the complexity of building LLM applications into composable, reusable components
  • The framework is provider-agnostic, supporting OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and many other model providers

Lesson 109: Business Applications of LangChain

LangChain solves real enterprise problems by providing modules for PII masking, document-grounded Q&A, and automated support workflows that companies like Ally Financial and Adyen deploy in production.

Core Concept

LangChain is not merely an academic exercise; it addresses concrete business needs across industries. Its modular architecture lets enterprises assemble LLM-powered pipelines that respect compliance requirements (such as PII masking), operate on proprietary data (through document retrieval), and automate repetitive knowledge work. Two representative case studies illustrate this. Ally Financial, a major US digital bank, uses LangChain to summarize customer-support call transcripts. Because financial conversations contain personally identifiable information (names, SSNs, account numbers), LangChain's PII-masking module strips sensitive data before passing text to the LLM, then re-inserts it into the final summary. Adyen, a fintech platform serving Microsoft, Spotify, and LinkedIn, uses LangChain to build an AI assistant that answers support questions grounded in their internal documentation, reducing resolution times and improving customer experience.

Key Points

  • Ally Financial uses LangChain to summarize call transcripts while masking PII (names, SSNs, account details) before LLM processing
  • PII masking is a built-in LangChain capability, not a separate third-party tool
  • Adyen uses LangChain for document-grounded Q&A, enabling support staff to query internal knowledge bases via an LLM
  • Both use cases demonstrate LangChain as a bridge between raw data and the LLM, handling preprocessing, security, and retrieval

Lesson 110: What Makes LangChain Powerful?

LangChain's power comes from its modular architecture: separate components for LLM integration, conversation memory, document loading and retrieval, and agent-based reasoning, all composable into a single application pipeline.

Core Concept

Building a production-grade LLM application requires far more than just calling a model API. A chatbot that remembers prior messages needs state management. One that answers questions about proprietary documents needs data loaders, vector stores, and retrieval logic. One that takes actions (searching the web, running code, querying databases) needs agent and tool frameworks. LangChain addresses each of these needs through dedicated, composable modules. For LLM access, it provides integrations with providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. For memory, it offers conversation storage backends that feed prior dialogue as context to the model. For context awareness, it supplies document loaders (PDF, CSV, DOCX, and more), text splitters, embedding models, and vector store integrations for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). For reasoning, it provides an agent framework that lets the model decide when and how to use external tools. LLMs are inherently stateless; every one of these features is an external mechanism that LangChain wires together.

Key Points

  • LLMs are inherently stateless; conversation memory is an external mechanism that stores and re-feeds prior dialogue
  • LangChain integrates with multiple LLM providers, making the underlying model swappable without code rewrites
  • Document loaders handle diverse data formats (PDF, CSV, DOCX) so heterogeneous data can be processed uniformly
  • Vector stores and embeddings enable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for grounding responses in proprietary data
  • Agents give the model the ability to reason about which tools to use, enabling autonomous task execution

LLM Integration

Swap between OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and other providers through a unified interface

Conversation Memory

Store and replay dialogue history so the chatbot maintains state across turns

Document Loaders & Retrieval

Ingest PDFs, CSVs, and other formats; embed and store in vector databases for RAG

Agents & Tools

Let the model reason about and invoke external tools (web search, code execution, APIs)

LangChain Expression Language

A composable protocol (LCEL) that chains all components into executable pipelines

💡 RAG Pipeline
Load documents, split into chunks, embed into a vector store, retrieve relevant context, and pass to LLM
💡 Agent with Tools
Model decides to search the web or query a database based on the user's question
Key Takeaways
  • Think of LangChain as a toolkit of interchangeable modules, not a monolithic framework
  • Every 'intelligent' chatbot feature (memory, grounding, tool use) is an external component that LangChain wires to the LLM

Lesson 111: What Does the Course Cover?

The course follows a structured progression: tokens and pricing, environment setup, raw OpenAI API usage, then each LangChain component (model I/O, memory, retrieval, agents, and LCEL) culminating in building a complete chatbot.

Core Concept

The learning path is designed as a bottom-up build. It begins with foundational concepts (how tokens work, how models are priced) before any code is written. The environment setup section ensures reproducible development with isolated Anaconda environments and secure API key management. Direct OpenAI API usage comes next, establishing familiarity with the raw interface that LangChain wraps. The bulk of the course then systematically covers each LangChain component: model inputs (prompts, prompt templates, few-shot examples), model outputs (output parsers that convert LLM responses into structured formats), chatbot memory (classes that maintain conversation state), document retrieval (loaders, embeddings, vector stores for RAG), and agents (tool-using, reasoning models). The LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) is the connective tissue that chains these components into executable pipelines.

Key Points

  • Tokens and pricing are covered first because cost awareness is essential before building applications
  • The OpenAI API is taught before LangChain to understand the underlying interface LangChain abstracts
  • LangChain components are covered individually: model I/O, memory, retrieval, agents, LCEL
  • Output parsers convert LLM string responses into structured Python objects (lists, dicts, datetime)

Section 23: Tokens, Models, and Prices

2 lectures

▼

Lesson 112: Tokens

Tokenization breaks text into sub-word units (tokens) that form the LLM's vocabulary; one token is roughly 3/4 of a word, so 100 tokens approximate 75 words, and this ratio governs both model capacity and cost.

Core Concept

Before an LLM can process text, it must convert the input into numerical representations. Tokenization is the process that breaks text into sequences of characters called tokens, which collectively form the model's vocabulary. A token is not necessarily a full word or a single character; it is a frequently co-occurring sequence of characters, typically about three-quarters of a word in English. The choice of token granularity is a design trade-off. Smaller tokens (closer to individual characters) produce a smaller vocabulary that is more memory-efficient and adapts more easily to new words or languages, but at the cost of making it harder for the model to capture semantic meaning, since predicting the next character conveys less information than predicting the next word. Larger tokens (full words or phrases) capture more meaning per prediction step but inflate the vocabulary and reduce flexibility. The sub-word tokenization used by models like GPT strikes a balance: common words become single tokens, while rare words are decomposed into smaller pieces. OpenAI provides a tokenizer tool (platform.openai.com/tokenizer) that visualizes how any given text is broken into tokens, letting developers estimate token counts before making API calls.

Key Points

  • One token is approximately 3/4 of a word; 100 tokens correspond to roughly 75 words
  • Tokens are sub-word units: common words map to one token, rare words are split into multiple tokens
  • Smaller tokens reduce vocabulary size and improve adaptability but weaken semantic capture per prediction
  • OpenAI's tokenizer tool (platform.openai.com/tokenizer) lets developers visualize and count tokens for any text
~0.75
Words per token (average in English)
100 tokens
Approximately 75 words
1M tokens
Approximately a 1,500-page novel
Sub-word
Token granularity: between characters and full words
💡 Token Visualization
The word 'Prompting' might be split into 'Prom' and 'pting' as two separate tokens depending on the tokenizer
Key Takeaways
  • Always estimate token counts before API calls; use OpenAI's tokenizer tool for precise counts
  • The 100-tokens-to-75-words rule of thumb is the fastest way to mentally estimate cost and context usage

Lesson 113: Models and Prices

OpenAI model selection involves balancing three factors: per-token price (input vs. output priced differently), training data cutoff date, and context window size, with GPT-4o offering the best performance-to-cost ratio at the time of writing.

Core Concept

OpenAI prices its API by token consumption, with input tokens and output tokens billed at different rates. Input tokens are those sent to the model as part of the prompt; output (or completion) tokens are those the model generates in response. Output tokens are consistently more expensive than input tokens because generation is computationally more intensive than encoding. At the time of writing, GPT-4o (GPT-4 Omni) is OpenAI's flagship model, priced at $5 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a training data cutoff of October 2023 and a context window of 128,000 tokens. GPT-4o Mini offers a cheaper alternative for simpler tasks. The context window is the total number of tokens (input plus output combined) that a single API call can handle; exceeding it requires truncation or chunking strategies. When selecting a model, three factors must be weighed: the per-token cost (which determines operational expense), the training data cutoff (which determines how current the model's knowledge is), and the context window (which determines how much text can be processed in a single call). For the API, pricing is token-based; the ChatGPT web interface, by contrast, uses subscription-based pricing where output verbosity does not affect cost.

Key Points

  • Input tokens and output tokens are priced differently; output tokens cost more due to higher computational cost
  • GPT-4o: $5/1M input tokens, $15/1M output tokens, 128K context window, October 2023 cutoff
  • The context window (128K tokens for GPT-4o) is shared between input and output; it is not input-only
  • API usage is token-based billing; ChatGPT web is subscription-based and not affected by output length
  • GPT-4o Mini provides a cost-effective option for tasks that do not require the full GPT-4o capability
$5
GPT-4o input cost per 1M tokens
$15
GPT-4o output cost per 1M tokens
128K
GPT-4o context window (input + output combined)
Oct 2023
GPT-4o training data cutoff date
3x
Output tokens are roughly 3x more expensive than input tokens
💡 Cost Estimation
1 million tokens (roughly a 1,500-page novel) of input to GPT-4o costs $5; the same volume of output costs $15
Key Takeaways
  • Control output length with max_tokens to avoid runaway costs from verbose model responses
  • Choose the smallest model that meets task requirements; GPT-4o Mini can handle many tasks at a fraction of GPT-4o cost

Section 24: Setting Up the Environment

3 lectures

Lesson 114: Setting Up a Custom Anaconda Environment for Jupyter Integration

Isolate project dependencies by creating a dedicated Anaconda environment, installing required packages, and registering it as a Jupyter kernel.

Core Concept

Project isolation through dedicated environments prevents dependency conflicts and ensures reproducibility. A fresh Anaconda environment with a specific Python version provides a clean slate for installing only the packages a project needs.

Key Points

  • Create environment: conda create --name langchain_env python=3.11
  • Activate: conda activate langchain_env
  • Install packages: pip install openai python-dotenv ipykernel jupyterlab notebook
  • Register as Jupyter kernel: python -m ipykernel install --user --name langchain_env
  • Verify: conda env list to confirm creation; kernel appears in Jupyter's kernel selector
Key Takeaways
  • Always create a new environment per project to avoid dependency conflicts
  • The ipykernel package is what makes a conda environment visible as a Jupyter kernel

Lesson 115: Obtaining an OpenAI API Key

Generate an API key from OpenAI's platform, save it immediately to a local file, and treat it as a secret credential that cannot be retrieved again once the creation dialog is closed.

Core Concept

Access to OpenAI's models via the API requires an API key, which is generated from the platform's settings page. The key is shown only once at creation time; closing the dialog makes it irretrievable, requiring generation of a new key if lost.

Key Points

  • Navigate to platform.openai.com > Settings > API Keys > Create new secret key
  • Copy the key immediately and save to a local text file before closing the dialog
  • The key is shown only once; losing it requires generating a replacement
  • A billing payment method must be configured before API calls will succeed
Key Takeaways
  • Save the API key to a secure file immediately upon generation; it cannot be displayed again
  • Set up billing before attempting any API calls

Lesson 116: Setting the API Key as an Environment Variable

Store the API key in a .env file and load it as an environment variable using python-dotenv, keeping credentials out of source code to prevent accidental exposure.

Core Concept

Environment variables are key-value pairs managed by the operating system. Storing the API key as an environment variable (rather than hard-coding it) prevents accidental exposure when sharing code. The python-dotenv library reads a .env file and injects its contents into the process environment, which the OpenAI library then reads automatically. Hard-coding API keys is a critical security risk: anyone with access to the source code can consume tokens at the key owner's expense. If abnormal usage is detected, the key should be revoked immediately from the OpenAI dashboard and a new one generated.

Key Points

  • Create a .env file containing OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... in the project directory
  • Load with python-dotenv: %load_ext dotenv then %dotenv in Jupyter, or dotenv.load_dotenv() in scripts
  • Access in code: os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']
  • Never hard-code API keys; revoke immediately if accidental exposure is suspected
Key Takeaways
  • The .env file should be in .gitignore to prevent committing credentials to version control
  • Revoking a compromised key instantly invalidates it; always generate a fresh replacement

Section 25: The OpenAI API

4 lectures

▼

Lesson 117: First Steps

The OpenAI API's core method is client.chat.completions.create(), which accepts a model name and a messages list of role/content dictionaries to produce a chat completion response.

Core Concept

The OpenAI Python library provides a structured interface for interacting with chat models. After initializing an OpenAI client (which reads the API key from the environment), the primary method for generating responses is client.chat.completions.create(). This method requires two key parameters: model (a string identifying which model to use, such as 'gpt-4o') and messages (a list of dictionaries, each containing a 'role' and 'content' key). The messages list defines the conversation context. Each dictionary specifies who is speaking (system, user, or assistant) and what they are saying. The model processes the entire messages list as context and generates a response. This stateless, request-response pattern means the developer is responsible for maintaining conversation history by accumulating messages across calls.

Key Points

  • Initialize client: client = OpenAI() (reads OPENAI_API_KEY from environment automatically)
  • Core call: client.chat.completions.create(model='gpt-4o', messages=[...])
  • The messages parameter is a list of dicts with 'role' (system/user/assistant) and 'content' (text) keys
  • Each API call is stateless; conversation history must be maintained by the developer
💡 Minimal Chat Completion
Pass a model name and a single user message dict to get a model response

💻 Code Walkthrough: 04-The-OpenAI-API-01.ipynb

Step 1

Next, we should configure the OpenAI library to recognize our key. To do so, import the os and openai libraries.

import os
import openai
Step 2

Then, set openai.api_key to equal os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'), passing the name of the environment variable as an argument.

We’re now ready to experiment with OpenAI’s models. We’ll do so by implementing a helpful chatbot that answers users’ questions. But we’ll also give it a sarcastic twist. 😊 First, create an OpenAI client by utilizing OpenAI’s class of the same name.

client = openai.OpenAI()
Step 4

Then, define a completion variable that will serve as our chatbot object. Set it equal to client.chat.completions.create. The first parameter that the create() function requires is the model. I’ll opt for GPT-4, but you can experiment with any OpenAI chat model. Just visit their website, pick a language model of your choice, and write the respective name as a string. Keep in mind our discussion about costs—especially if you plan on working on your own projects. Opt for a cost-sensitive model variant when working on personal projects. The second required parameter (messages) contains the messages we’ll give the model before starting the conversation. These messages will be a way to instruct the model on how to behave. It expects a list of dictionaries, each containing two required key-value pairs.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{}, 
                                                        {}])
Key Takeaways
  • The messages list is the conversation; the model has no memory beyond what is explicitly passed
  • Understanding this raw API pattern is essential before using LangChain, which wraps it

Lesson 118: System, User, and Assistant Roles

The three message roles serve distinct purposes: system sets the model's persona and constraints, user provides the human's input, and assistant supplies example responses or prior context for few-shot guidance.

Core Concept

Every message in the OpenAI chat completions API carries a role that tells the model how to interpret it. The system role defines the model's identity, behavior, output format, and constraints. It is processed as meta-instructions that shape all subsequent responses. For example, a system message might instruct the model to act as a grammar corrector, a sarcastic chatbot, or a sentiment classifier. The user role represents the human's input: questions, requests, or content to be processed. The assistant role represents the model's own prior responses. When used proactively (before the model has responded), assistant messages serve as example outputs that demonstrate the desired response style or format. This is the mechanism behind few-shot prompting at the API level: alternating user and assistant messages create input-output pairs the model learns from in-context. For a sentiment classifier, a developer might provide a system message defining the task, then several user messages (example tweets) each followed by an assistant message (the classification: positive, neutral, or negative). The model infers the pattern and applies it to new user messages.

Key Points

  • System role: sets persona, constraints, output format; processed as meta-instructions that shape all responses
  • User role: the human's question, request, or content to be processed
  • Assistant role: model's prior responses or developer-supplied example outputs for few-shot prompting
  • Few-shot prompting at the API level uses alternating user/assistant message pairs as examples
Role Purpose Who Provides It When to Use
system Define model persona, behavior, and constraints Developer Once at the start of every conversation to set context
user Submit questions, requests, or content End user (or developer in examples) Every turn where human input is needed
assistant Provide example outputs or recall prior responses Developer (examples) or model (actual responses) Few-shot prompting or maintaining conversation history
💡 Sentiment Classifier
System defines the task; user/assistant pairs demonstrate 'This movie is extraordinary' -> 'Positive' as examples
💡 Sarcastic Persona
System message 'You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers with sarcastic responses' shapes all outputs
Key Takeaways
  • Always include a system message; it dramatically improves response quality for specific use cases
  • Few-shot prompting is just alternating user/assistant messages that demonstrate the desired input-output pattern

Lesson 119: Creating a Sarcastic Chatbot

A chat completion response is a ChatCompletion object containing a choices list; the generated text is accessed at completion.choices[0].message.content, and the response also reports token usage for cost tracking.

Core Concept

When client.chat.completions.create() is called, it returns a ChatCompletion object rather than a plain string. This object contains structured metadata alongside the generated text. The key attribute is choices, a list of Choice objects (by default containing one item, controllable via the n parameter). Each Choice contains a message object with role (always 'assistant' for generated responses) and content (the actual text). The standard access pattern is: completion.choices[0].message.content. The ChatCompletion object also includes a usage attribute reporting prompt_tokens (input), completion_tokens (output), and total_tokens, enabling cost tracking per request. Increasing n generates multiple alternative responses but multiplies token consumption proportionally.

Key Points

  • Response structure: ChatCompletion > choices (list) > Choice > message > content (string)
  • Access pattern: completion.choices[0].message.content
  • The n parameter controls how many alternative responses are generated (default: 1)
  • Token usage is reported in the response: prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, and total_tokens
  • The generated message always has role='assistant'
💡 Sarcastic Bot Implementation
System message sets sarcastic persona; user message asks for dog name suggestions; response extracted via .choices[0].message.content

💻 Code Walkthrough: 04-The-OpenAI-API-03.ipynb

Step 1

Creating a sarcastic chatbot: set the system role to define persona, then pass user messages for response.

import os
import openai
Step 2

Setting up dependencies. os: system environment variables.

openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')
Step 3

Importing required libraries.

client = openai.OpenAI()
Step 4

Now, the first dictionary in our messages list should map the ‘role’ keyword to ‘system’, implying a system message. In addition, set the content to the one already familiar to you: *You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers questions with sarcastic responses.* In the second dictionary in the list, we’ll create a user message. I’ll go with the following request: *I’ve recently adopted a dog. Could you suggest some dog names?*

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' I've recently adopted a dog. 
                                                         Could you suggest some dog names? '''}])
Step 5

Run the cell above and inspect the completion variable.

completion
Step 6

Finally, for this lesson, let’s check how the chatbot responded by displaying the output in a more readable form. To do that:

  • first, retrieve the choices list from the ChatCompletion object,
  • then select the first and only item in this list,
  • fetch the messages parameter from the Choice object,
  • and lastly, extract the content from the ChatCompletionMessage object.
Apply the print function to format the output string cleanly.

print(completion.choices[0].message.content)
Key Takeaways
  • Always extract content via completion.choices[0].message.content, not by printing the raw completion object
  • Monitor the usage attribute on every response to track and control API costs

Lesson 120: Temperature, Max Tokens, and Streaming

Three critical parameters control response behavior: max_tokens caps output length to manage cost, temperature (0 to 2) controls randomness vs. determinism, and stream=True delivers tokens incrementally for real-time display.

Core Concept

Beyond model and messages, three parameters in chat.completions.create() give fine-grained control over response generation. The max_tokens parameter (also called max_completion_tokens) sets an upper bound on the number of output tokens the model can generate. This directly controls cost and prevents verbose responses. Setting it too low, however, can truncate the response mid-sentence. Finding the right value requires balancing completeness against cost. The temperature parameter accepts values from 0 to 2 and controls the randomness of the model's token selection. At temperature 0, the model always selects the highest-probability token, producing deterministic, focused outputs ideal for factual or classification tasks. As temperature increases toward 2, the model samples more broadly from its probability distribution, producing more creative, varied, and sometimes surprising outputs suitable for brainstorming or creative writing. The default is typically 1. The stream parameter, when set to True, changes the response from a single completed object to an iterator that yields tokens (or small chunks) as they are generated. This enables real-time display of responses in user interfaces, reducing perceived latency for long outputs. The developer iterates over the stream and concatenates the chunks to build the complete response.

Key Points

  • max_tokens caps output length; too low truncates responses, too high wastes cost on verbose outputs
  • temperature=0: deterministic, highest-probability tokens; ideal for factual/classification tasks
  • temperature=1: balanced creativity (default); temperature=2: maximum randomness and creativity
  • stream=True returns an iterator yielding chunks as they are generated, enabling real-time display
  • API pricing is token-based; ChatGPT web is subscription-based and unaffected by output length
Parameter Type Range Default Effect
max_tokens int 1 to model max Model-dependent Caps output token count; controls cost and response length
temperature float 0 to 2 1 0 = deterministic/focused; 2 = highly random/creative
stream bool True / False False True = incremental token delivery; False = single response object
n int 1+ 1 Number of alternative responses generated; multiplies token cost
💡 Max Tokens Effect
Same prompt with max_tokens=250 produces a complete answer; max_tokens=50 produces a truncated, incomplete one
💡 Streaming Response
Iterating over the stream object and printing each chunk as it arrives creates a typewriter effect

for i in completion:
    print(i.choices[0].delta.content, end = "")

Section 26: Model Inputs

7 lectures

▼

Lesson 121: The LangChain Framework

LangChain organizes LLM application development into five component groups: Model I/O (prompts, templates, parsers), Memory, Retrieval, Agents, and LCEL (LangChain Expression Language), each addressing a distinct architectural concern.

Core Concept

The LangChain framework decomposes the complex task of building LLM-powered applications into five modular component groups, each responsible for a specific concern. Model I/O encompasses everything related to interacting with the language model itself: the LLM integration, prompt construction (including prompt templates for reusability and example selectors for few-shot prompting), and output parsers that convert raw model responses into structured Python objects. Memory components maintain conversation state across turns, since LLMs are inherently stateless. Retrieval components handle loading documents from various formats, splitting them into chunks, embedding them into vector representations, and storing/querying them in vector databases for retrieval-augmented generation. Agent components give the model the ability to reason about and invoke external tools. The LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) is the protocol that composes all of these components into executable pipelines using a declarative chaining syntax. Prompt templates are a key abstraction within Model I/O. They convert hardcoded prompt strings into reusable templates with placeholders (input variables) that can be filled at runtime. This makes prompts parameterizable and composable, which is essential for few-shot prompting and dynamic prompt construction.

Key Points

  • Model I/O: LLM, prompts, prompt templates, example selectors, and output parsers
  • Prompt templates turn static prompts into reusable templates with {placeholder} variables
  • Output parsers convert raw LLM string responses into structured formats (lists, dicts, datetime objects)
  • Memory, Retrieval, Agents, and LCEL are the other four component groups
  • LCEL is the composable protocol that chains components into executable pipelines

Model I/O

Prompt templates, few-shot examples, LLM calls, and output parsers for structured responses

Memory

Conversation state management: store and replay dialogue history across turns

Retrieval

Document loaders, text splitters, embeddings, and vector stores for RAG

Agents & Tools

LLM-driven reasoning that selects and invokes external tools autonomously

LCEL

LangChain Expression Language: declarative pipe syntax for composing components into chains

💡 Prompt Template Reuse
Replace 'dog' with a {pet} placeholder to reuse the same prompt for dogs, cats, or any animal
Key Takeaways
  • Prompt templates are the entry point to LangChain; they make prompts parameterizable and reusable
  • LCEL is the glue that connects every LangChain component; understanding it unlocks the entire framework

Lesson 122: ChatOpenAI

The ChatOpenAI class is LangChain's wrapper around OpenAI's chat models; it is instantiated with model parameters and invoked via .invoke(), accepting a string or message list and returning an AIMessage object.

Core Concept

LangChain's integration with OpenAI's chat models is provided by the ChatOpenAI class, imported from langchain_openai.chat_models. This class wraps the raw OpenAI API into LangChain's unified interface, enabling seamless composition with other LangChain components. Instantiation requires specifying the model (e.g., 'gpt-4o'), and optionally temperature and max_tokens (passed via model_kwargs or directly). Once instantiated, the .invoke() method is the primary interface for generating responses. In its simplest form, .invoke() accepts a plain string and returns an AIMessage object containing the model's response in its .content attribute. The ChatOpenAI class automatically reads the OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment, so no explicit key passing is needed. Two packages must be installed: langchain (the core framework) and langchain-openai (the OpenAI-specific integration). This separation allows LangChain to support multiple providers without requiring all provider packages to be installed.

Key Points

  • Import: from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI
  • Instantiation: chat = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o', temperature=0, max_tokens=100)
  • Invocation: chat.invoke('your question') returns an AIMessage object
  • AIMessage.content contains the response text as a string
  • Two packages required: langchain (core) and langchain-openai (provider integration)
💡 Simple String Invocation
chat.invoke('Suggest dog names') returns an AIMessage whose .content holds the model's response text

Lesson 123: System and Human Messages

LangChain provides typed message classes (SystemMessage, HumanMessage) that replace raw role/content dictionaries, enabling type safety and composability when invoking chat models with .invoke([messages]).

Core Concept

While the raw OpenAI API uses dictionaries with 'role' and 'content' keys, LangChain provides dedicated Python classes for each message type, imported from langchain_core.messages. SystemMessage wraps the system role, defining the model's persona, behavior, and constraints. HumanMessage wraps the user role, carrying the human's question or request. To invoke a chat model with multiple messages, pass a list of message objects to .invoke(): chat.invoke([system_msg, human_msg]). The model processes them in order, using the system message as behavioral context and the human message as the prompt to respond to. The return value is an AIMessage object whose .content attribute holds the response text. Using typed message classes instead of raw dictionaries provides several advantages: IDE autocompletion, type checking, and seamless integration with LangChain's prompt template system. The message objects are also directly composable with chains and other LangChain abstractions.

Key Points

  • Import: from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage
  • SystemMessage(content='...') replaces {'role': 'system', 'content': '...'}
  • HumanMessage(content='...') replaces {'role': 'user', 'content': '...'}
  • Invoke with a list: chat.invoke([system_msg, human_msg]) returns AIMessage
  • Typed classes enable IDE support, type safety, and seamless composition with LangChain components
LangChain Class OpenAI API Equivalent Purpose Import Path
SystemMessage {'role': 'system', ...} Set model persona, behavior, and constraints langchain_core.messages
HumanMessage {'role': 'user', ...} Carry the human's question or request langchain_core.messages
AIMessage {'role': 'assistant', ...} Model response or developer-supplied example output langchain_core.messages

Lesson 124: AI Messages

AIMessage objects represent model-generated responses and can also be used proactively to implement few-shot prompting, where alternating HumanMessage/AIMessage pairs teach the model the desired response pattern through in-context examples.

Core Concept

The AIMessage class serves a dual purpose in LangChain. First, it is the type of the object returned by chat.invoke(), containing the model's generated response. Second, it can be instantiated by the developer and included in the messages list to provide example responses, implementing few-shot prompting. Few-shot prompting is the technique of providing the model with a set of example input-output pairs so that it infers the desired response pattern. Rather than explicitly instructing the model with a system message (e.g., 'be sarcastic'), the developer can demonstrate the desired behavior through examples: a HumanMessage with a question followed by an AIMessage with the desired sarcastic response. Multiple such pairs train the model in-context without any fine-tuning. In practice, combining both approaches (a system message for explicit instructions plus a few example pairs for demonstration) produces the most reliable results. Pure few-shot prompting without a system message works but is less robust than the combined approach. The key insight is that AIMessage is not just an output container; it is an active input tool for shaping model behavior.

Key Points

  • AIMessage is both the return type of .invoke() and an input type for few-shot examples
  • Few-shot prompting: alternating HumanMessage/AIMessage pairs demonstrate desired input-output patterns
  • Zero-shot: no examples provided; the model relies entirely on the system message or its training
  • Best practice: combine a system message (explicit instructions) with few-shot examples (demonstrated behavior)
  • Import: from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage

Zero-Shot

No examples; model relies on system message and training data alone

Few-Shot

2-5 HumanMessage/AIMessage pairs demonstrate the desired response pattern

System + Few-Shot

Explicit instructions via SystemMessage combined with example pairs for maximum reliability

AIMessage Dual Role

Serves as both the model's output container and a developer-supplied input for examples

💡 Few-Shot Sarcasm
Two HumanMessage/AIMessage pairs demonstrating sarcastic responses teach the model the style without explicit instructions

Lesson 125: Prompt Templates and Prompt Values

PromptTemplate creates reusable prompt strings with {placeholder} variables; calling .invoke() with a dictionary of values fills the placeholders and returns a StringPromptValue object that can be passed directly to a chat model.

Core Concept

Hardcoded prompt strings are inflexible: changing a single word requires editing the entire string. LangChain's PromptTemplate class solves this by introducing parameterized templates with input variables enclosed in curly braces. A PromptTemplate is created using the .from_template() class method, which parses the string to identify input variables automatically. For example, a template string like 'I recently adopted a {pet}. Could you suggest some {pet} names?' has one input variable: 'pet'. Calling .invoke({'pet': 'dog'}) on the template fills the placeholders and returns a StringPromptValue object. The StringPromptValue is an intermediate representation that bridges prompt templates and chat models. It wraps the filled-in string and can be converted to a plain string (via .to_string()) or to a list of messages (via .to_messages(), which wraps the string in a HumanMessage). This dual conversion capability means a single PromptTemplate output can be fed to either a string-based LLM or a chat-based model. The convention of naming template strings in ALL_CAPS (e.g., TEMPLATE = '...') is a common developer practice for distinguishing templates from regular variables.

Key Points

  • Create: PromptTemplate.from_template('I adopted a {pet}. Suggest {pet} names?')
  • Input variables are auto-detected from {placeholder} syntax in the template string
  • Invoke: prompt_template.invoke({'pet': 'dog'}) returns a StringPromptValue
  • StringPromptValue can be converted to a string (.to_string()) or messages list (.to_messages())
  • Import: from langchain_core.prompts import PromptTemplate
1
Define Template String
Write a string with {placeholders} for variable parts
2
Create PromptTemplate
PromptTemplate.from_template(string) auto-detects input variables
3
Invoke with Values
.invoke({'var': 'value'}) fills placeholders, returns StringPromptValue
4
Convert or Pass
.to_string() for plain text or .to_messages() for chat model input
💡 Parameterized Pet Names
A {pet} placeholder lets the same template generate prompts for dogs, cats, or any animal without rewriting

Lesson 126: Chat Prompt Templates and Chat Prompt Values

ChatPromptTemplate composes typed message templates (SystemMessagePromptTemplate, HumanMessagePromptTemplate) into a reusable multi-message prompt; invoking it returns a ChatPromptValue containing properly typed message objects ready for a chat model.

Core Concept

While PromptTemplate works with plain strings, real chat applications need to construct multi-message prompts with distinct system and human roles. LangChain provides message-specific prompt template classes: SystemMessagePromptTemplate and HumanMessagePromptTemplate, each wrapping a PromptTemplate internally and associating it with the correct message type. Each message template is created via .from_template(), just like PromptTemplate. The key class that composes them is ChatPromptTemplate, created with ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([system_template, human_template]). This aggregates multiple message templates into a single, multi-message prompt template. Invoking a ChatPromptTemplate with a dictionary of input values returns a ChatPromptValue object. Unlike StringPromptValue, ChatPromptValue contains a list of typed message objects (SystemMessage, HumanMessage, etc.) with all placeholders filled. This ChatPromptValue can be passed directly to chat.invoke(), completing the prompt-to-model pipeline. This layered architecture (string templates inside message templates inside chat prompt templates) provides maximum reusability: the same system template can be composed with different human templates, and vice versa.

Key Points

  • SystemMessagePromptTemplate.from_template('{description}') creates a reusable system message template
  • HumanMessagePromptTemplate.from_template('Suggest {pet} names?') creates a reusable human message template
  • ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([sys_tmpl, human_tmpl]) composes them into a multi-message prompt
  • Invoke: chat_prompt.invoke({'description': '...', 'pet': 'dog'}) returns ChatPromptValue
  • ChatPromptValue.to_messages() returns a list of typed message objects; passable directly to chat.invoke()
Class Input Output Use Case
PromptTemplate String with {vars} StringPromptValue Single-string prompts or building block for message templates
SystemMessagePromptTemplate PromptTemplate (auto-created) Part of ChatPromptValue as SystemMessage Reusable system instructions with placeholders
HumanMessagePromptTemplate PromptTemplate (auto-created) Part of ChatPromptValue as HumanMessage Reusable user prompts with placeholders
ChatPromptTemplate List of message templates ChatPromptValue (list of typed messages) Complete multi-message prompt composition
💡 Sarcastic Pet Bot Template
System template with {description} placeholder and human template with {pet} placeholder compose into a reusable ChatPromptTemplate

Lesson 127: Few-Shot Chat Message Prompt Templates

FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate replaces manual HumanMessage/AIMessage pair construction with a scalable, data-driven approach where examples are stored as a list of dictionaries and automatically expanded into typed message pairs.

Core Concept

Manual few-shot prompting (creating individual HumanMessage and AIMessage objects for each example) becomes unwieldy as the number of examples grows. LangChain's FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate provides a scalable alternative by separating the example data from the template structure. The implementation has three parts. First, define a ChatPromptTemplate that represents the structure of a single example (one HumanMessage template and one AIMessage template). Second, prepare the examples as a list of dictionaries, where each dictionary maps the template's input variables to concrete values. Third, create a FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate by passing the example template and the examples list. When invoked, the FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate iterates over the examples list, applies each dictionary to the template, and produces the corresponding sequence of typed messages. This output can be embedded within a larger ChatPromptTemplate (alongside a system message and a final human message) to create a complete few-shot prompt. This design cleanly separates data (the examples list) from structure (the template), making it trivial to add, remove, or modify examples without touching the prompt logic. It also opens the door to dynamic example selection, where an ExampleSelector chooses the most relevant examples at runtime based on the user's input.

Key Points

  • Import: from langchain_core.prompts import FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate
  • Define an example template: ChatPromptTemplate combining HumanMessagePromptTemplate and AIMessagePromptTemplate
  • Examples are a list of dicts: [{'input': '...', 'response': '...'}, ...]
  • FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate(example_prompt=template, examples=examples_list)
  • Embed within a larger ChatPromptTemplate using .from_messages([system, few_shot_template, final_human])
  • Separating data from structure makes examples easy to modify and enables dynamic example selection

Lesson 128: String Output Parser

The StrOutputParser extracts the plain-text content from an AIMessage object, converting it to a Python string for downstream processing.

Core Concept

Chat model classes in LangChain return AIMessage objects by default. While these objects carry useful metadata, many downstream tasks require raw text. The StrOutputParser is the simplest output parser: it takes an AIMessage (or any BaseMessage) and returns just the string stored in its `.content` attribute. Usage follows a two-step pattern. First, invoke the chat model to obtain an AIMessage. Then call `StrOutputParser().invoke(response)` on that message to extract the plain string. This parser is foundational because it appears at the end of nearly every LCEL chain, converting the model's structured response object into a clean string suitable for display, storage, or further text manipulation.

Key Points

  • Chat models output AIMessage objects, not raw strings; an output parser bridges this gap.
  • StrOutputParser.invoke() accepts an AIMessage and returns the .content field as a Python str.
  • Output parsers themselves are Runnable objects, so they support invoke(), stream(), and batch().
  • StrOutputParser is the default 'last link' in most LCEL chains.
1
Invoke Chat Model
chat.invoke([HumanMessage(...)]) returns an AIMessage object
2
Apply StrOutputParser
parser.invoke(ai_message) extracts .content as a Python string
3
Use Result
The output is a plain str ready for display or further processing
💡 Basic String Extraction
Invoke a chat model, then pass the AIMessage to StrOutputParser().invoke() to get plain text.

Lesson 129: Comma-Separated List Output Parser

The CommaSeparatedListOutputParser parses an LLM response into a Python list, but requires injecting format instructions into the prompt so the model outputs comma-separated values.

Core Concept

When the desired output is a Python list of discrete items (names, tags, keywords), the CommaSeparatedListOutputParser provides an end-to-end solution. However, unlike StrOutputParser, it cannot operate on arbitrary model output. The model must be explicitly instructed to format its response as comma-separated values; otherwise, the parser receives a numbered list or paragraph and produces a single-element list instead of the intended multi-element result. Every LangChain output parser exposes a `get_format_instructions()` method that returns a human-readable string describing the required output format. This instruction string should be embedded directly into the prompt template, typically via an f-string or template variable. The resulting prompt tells the LLM exactly how to structure its answer so the parser can reliably split it into list elements. This pattern of 'inject instructions, then parse' is the universal workflow for all structured output parsers in LangChain.

Key Points

  • Without format instructions in the prompt, the model outputs free-form text that the parser cannot split correctly.
  • get_format_instructions() returns a string like 'Your response should be a list of comma separated values, e.g.: foo, bar, baz'.
  • The instruction string is embedded into the prompt template so the LLM knows the expected format before generating.
  • After the model responds in the correct format, parser.invoke(response) returns a Python list of strings.
1
Get Format Instructions
parser.get_format_instructions() produces a formatting directive string
2
Embed in Prompt
Append the instruction string to the prompt template via f-string or placeholder
3
Invoke Model
The LLM receives the formatted prompt and responds with comma-separated values
4
Parse Response
parser.invoke(response) splits the CSV string into a Python list

Lesson 130: Datetime Output Parser

The DatetimeOutputParser converts an LLM's textual date response into a Python datetime object, but requires strict format instructions to ensure the model outputs only a parseable date string.

Core Concept

The DatetimeOutputParser extends the inject-then-parse pattern to temporal data. It instructs the model to respond with a date/time in a specific format (e.g., `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%fZ`) and nothing else. The parser then converts that string into a Python `datetime` object, enabling programmatic date arithmetic, comparison, and formatting. Without format instructions, the model typically responds with a full sentence ('The poet was born on December 17, 1905'), which cannot be parsed into a datetime. Injecting `get_format_instructions()` into the prompt constrains the model to output only the date string in the required format. This lesson reinforces a critical principle: the more structured the desired output, the more precise the prompt instructions must be. An OutputParserException is raised when the response does not match the expected pattern, providing clear feedback for debugging.

Key Points

  • DatetimeOutputParser expects a date string in a specific strftime format, with no surrounding text.
  • An OutputParserException is raised if the model's response does not match the expected datetime pattern.
  • get_format_instructions() for this parser specifies the exact format string and instructs the model to return only the date.
  • The parsed result is a native Python datetime object, enabling arithmetic and comparison operations.
Parser Input Type Output Type Format Instructions Required Use Case
StrOutputParser AIMessage str No Extract plain text from any model response
CommaSeparatedListOutputParser AIMessage List[str] Yes Parse enumerated items into a Python list
DatetimeOutputParser AIMessage datetime Yes (strict) Convert date answers into datetime objects
💡 Historical Date Query
Ask when a poet was born with format instructions; parser returns a datetime(1905, 12, 17, ...) object.

Section 28: LangChain Module: LangChain Expression Language (LCEL)

10 lectures
