Lesson 168: Conditional Edges: Building the Graph

Conditional edges are added via add_conditional_edges(source, path, path_map) where path is the routing function; using Literal return types or an explicit path_map ensures correct graph visualization with dashed conditional edges.

Core Concept

The `add_conditional_edges()` method connects a source node to multiple possible targets via a routing function. It takes two required keyword arguments: `source` (the origin node name) and `path` (the routing callable). An optional `path_map` argument provides an explicit dictionary mapping return values to node names, which is especially useful for graph visualization. Without either `path_map` or a `Literal` return type on the routing function, the compiled graph's visualization may fail to show the branching structure. Two solutions exist: (1) provide `path_map={'yes': 'ask_question', 'no': '__end__'}` to explicitly declare the routes, or (2) annotate the routing function's return type with `Literal['ask_question', '__end__']`, which LangGraph uses to infer the possible targets. Both approaches produce dashed edges in the visualization, visually distinguishing conditional edges from direct ones. After building, the graph is invoked with an initial state. A key observation at this stage: the graph does not retain messages between nodes. Each state update overwrites the previous content, meaning the chatbot cannot remember earlier questions. This limitation motivates the next section on message management.

Key Points

  • add_conditional_edges() requires source (origin node) and path (routing function)
  • path_map explicitly maps routing function return values to target node names for visualization
  • Alternatively, a Literal return type on the routing function lets LangGraph infer possible targets
  • Conditional edges render as dashed lines in graph visualizations, distinguishing them from direct edges
Approach Mechanism Visualization Effect
path_map argument Explicit dict mapping return values to node names Shows dashed conditional edges with labeled targets
Literal return type Type hint restricts routing function output to specific node names LangGraph infers targets; renders dashed edges automatically
Neither (plain string) Routing function returns a generic string Visualization may not show branching correctly
💡 Visualization fix
Adding path_map or Literal return type causes the graph diagram to correctly show branching after the conditional node

6 lectures

Lesson 169: The Annotated Construct and Reducer Functions

The Annotated type hint combined with the add_messages reducer function changes the default state update behavior from overwriting to appending, enabling conversation history accumulation across nodes.

Core Concept

By default, when a LangGraph node returns an updated state, the new value replaces the old value for each key. This is problematic for chatbot memory: each node's output overwrites the previous messages rather than building a conversation history. The solution lies in two constructs used together: `Annotated` from Python's `typing` module and the `add_messages` function from `langgraph.graph`. The `add_messages` function is a reducer: it takes two arguments (the existing message list and the new messages) and returns a merged list rather than replacing the old with the new. When the state schema annotates its `messages` field as `Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages]`, LangGraph intercepts every state update to that key and applies the reducer instead of performing a raw overwrite. The `Annotated` construct itself is a Python typing feature that attaches metadata to a type hint without changing the underlying type. The variable is still `Sequence[BaseMessage]`, but the attached `add_messages` metadata instructs LangGraph on how to merge updates. This pattern is the foundation of all conversation memory in LangGraph.

Key Points

  • Default state update behavior is overwrite: new values replace old values entirely
  • Annotated attaches metadata to a type hint without changing the underlying type
  • add_messages is a reducer function that merges new messages into the existing list instead of replacing
  • The pattern Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages] is the standard way to enable message accumulation
Behavior Without Annotated + Reducer With Annotated + add_messages
State update New value overwrites old value New messages are appended to existing list
Conversation history Lost after each node Accumulates across all nodes
Schema definition messages: Sequence[BaseMessage] messages: Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages]
Use case Single-turn responses Multi-turn conversations with memory
💡 add_messages demo
add_messages([HumanMessage('Hi'), AIMessage('Hello')], [HumanMessage('News?')]) returns a list of all three messages

Lesson 170: Reducer Functions in Action

With the add_messages reducer in place, each node appends its messages to the growing state list, and the routing function must reference the last message (index -1) rather than the first to check the most recent user response.

Core Concept

Once the `Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages]` pattern is applied to the state schema, the practical effect becomes visible during graph execution. Every node that returns a state with new messages causes those messages to be appended to the existing list rather than replacing it. This means the message list grows continuously as the conversation progresses through nodes. This accumulation has a downstream implication for routing functions. When the state contained only the latest messages (under the default overwrite behavior), checking the first message (index 0) was sufficient. With appending, the most recent user response is now at the end of the list, so the routing function must reference index -1 instead. Pretty-printing messages at each node provides visibility into the growing state, confirming that the conversation history is being preserved. The graph now retains full context: the chatbot can answer follow-up questions that reference earlier exchanges, such as knowing which poet the user asked about in a previous turn.

Key Points

  • With add_messages, each node's returned messages are appended, growing the list continuously
  • Routing functions must shift from checking index 0 to index -1 to inspect the latest message
  • Pretty-printing messages at each node helps verify that the reducer is working as expected
  • The chatbot can now answer context-dependent follow-up questions because history is preserved
1
Node 1: Ask Question
Appends AI prompt + HumanMessage with user input to state
2
Node 2: Chatbot
Invokes LLM with full message history; appends AIMessage response
3
Node 3: Ask Another
Appends follow-up prompt + user's yes/no response
4
Routing Check
Reads state['messages'][-1] to decide: loop back or terminate
💡 Follow-up context retention
After asking about a poet, the user can ask 'where was the poet born?' and the chatbot knows which poet is referenced

Lesson 171: The MessagesState Class

MessagesState is a pre-built LangGraph class that provides the most common state configuration out of the box: a messages key of sequence type with the add_messages reducer, eliminating the need for manual TypedDict and Annotated definitions.

Core Concept

Defining a state as a TypedDict with an `Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages]` field is the most common pattern in LangGraph chatbot applications. Because this pattern is so prevalent, LangGraph provides a convenience class called `MessagesState` (importable from `langgraph.graph`) that encapsulates it. This class already has a `messages` key of the correct sequence type with the `add_messages` reducer pre-configured. Using `MessagesState` simplifies code: the custom state class definition can be removed entirely, and all node functions simply accept and return `MessagesState` objects. The `StateGraph` constructor also takes `MessagesState` directly as its schema argument. The class is designed to be extensible; it can be subclassed to add additional keys (such as a `summary` field) while retaining the built-in message management behavior. This extensibility becomes critical when implementing summarization strategies later in the pipeline.

Key Points

  • MessagesState is a pre-built class with messages key, sequence type, and add_messages reducer included
  • It eliminates boilerplate: no need to manually define TypedDict + Annotated for the common case
  • All node functions and the StateGraph constructor can use MessagesState directly
  • MessagesState is subclassable; additional keys can be added while preserving built-in message handling

Lesson 172: The RemoveMessages Class

RemoveMessages is a LangChain message class that, when passed through the add_messages reducer, deletes messages with matching IDs from the state, enabling selective message removal by construction rather than by mutation.

Core Concept

As conversations grow, sending the entire message history to the LLM becomes expensive in both tokens and latency. LangGraph provides a mechanism for selective message removal through the `RemoveMessage` class from `langchain_core.messages`. The approach is counterintuitive: messages are "removed" by adding `RemoveMessage` objects to the state. The process works as follows. The `add_messages` function assigns a unique ID to each message when it first enters the state. To delete specific messages, a list of `RemoveMessage` objects is created, each initialized with the `id` of a target message. When this list is passed through the `add_messages` reducer, the reducer matches IDs and removes the corresponding messages from the state. This enables a trimming pattern: to keep only the last N messages, create `RemoveMessage` objects for everything except the final N entries, then return those through the reducer. The mechanism is declarative rather than imperative: instead of mutating the list directly, the developer describes which messages to remove and lets the reducer handle the operation.

Key Points

  • add_messages assigns a unique ID to each message entering the state
  • RemoveMessage objects specify target message IDs; the reducer deletes matching messages
  • The pattern is 'remove by adding': RemoveMessage objects passed through add_messages trigger deletion
  • This enables keeping only the last N messages by creating RemoveMessage objects for all earlier ones
1
Messages Accumulate
add_messages assigns unique IDs to each message as they enter the state
2
Identify Targets
Select messages to remove (e.g., all except the last 5) by their IDs
3
Create RemoveMessage Objects
For each target, create RemoveMessage(id=message.id)
4
Pass Through Reducer
Return RemoveMessage list as state update; add_messages deletes matching IDs
💡 Keep last 5 messages

Lesson 173: Trimming Messages

A dedicated trim_messages node uses RemoveMessage objects to keep only the last N messages in the state before looping back, preserving recent context but losing earlier conversation details.

Core Concept

Message trimming is implemented as a dedicated graph node inserted into the conversation loop. The `trim_messages` node accepts the current state, identifies all messages except the last N (typically 5), creates `RemoveMessage` objects for each one, and returns them through the state. The `add_messages` reducer then removes the targeted messages, leaving only the most recent exchanges. The trimming node is placed between the "ask another question" node and the "ask question" node in the loop path. When the routing function determines the user wants to continue, the graph routes through `trim_messages` before prompting for a new question. This keeps the message list bounded regardless of how many loop iterations occur. The trade-off is significant: trimming preserves recent context (the chatbot knows the current topic) but loses earlier details. If the user asks about something discussed several turns ago that has been trimmed, the chatbot will not recall it. This limitation motivates the more sophisticated summarization approach.

Key Points

  • The trim node sits in the loop path, executing before each new question prompt
  • It keeps the last N messages (e.g., 5) and removes all earlier ones via RemoveMessage
  • Trimming bounds memory usage but introduces context loss for older conversation turns
  • The chatbot retains awareness of the current topic but loses details from trimmed messages
Aspect No Trimming (Full History) With Trimming (Last N)
Memory usage Grows unbounded with each turn Capped at N messages
Token consumption Increases every turn; expensive for long conversations Constant per invocation
Context retention Complete conversation history available Only last N messages; earlier context lost
Suitability Short conversations Medium-length conversations where recent context suffices
💡 Context loss demonstration
After trimming, asking 'do you remember the grook you told me?' fails because that message was removed from state

Lesson 174: Summarizing Messages

Message summarization replaces the trim-and-lose approach with a strategy that condenses all prior messages into a running summary stored in a separate state key, then deletes the raw messages, preserving context without unbounded token growth.

Core Concept

Summarization is the most sophisticated message management strategy in LangGraph. It addresses the core limitation of trimming (context loss) by condensing the conversation into a running summary before deleting the raw messages. The implementation requires three changes to the graph architecture. First, the state schema is extended by subclassing `MessagesState` and adding a `summary` key of type `str`. Critically, this key is NOT annotated with a reducer, so each update overwrites the previous summary (which is the desired behavior; the summary is replaced, not appended). Second, the chatbot node is modified to include the running summary as a system message alongside the user's question, giving the LLM context from earlier in the conversation. The `dict.get('summary', '')` method safely retrieves the summary, returning an empty string if none exists yet. Third, a "summarize and delete" node replaces the trim node. It formats the entire current conversation into a readable string, instructs the LLM to update the existing summary with this new information, stores the result in the `summary` key, and then deletes all messages from state via `RemoveMessage` objects. This approach retains the essence of the entire conversation in a compact form while keeping token consumption bounded.

Key Points

  • The state is extended with a summary key (plain str, no reducer) that gets overwritten each update
  • The chatbot node injects the summary as a SystemMessage to provide historical context to the LLM
  • dict.get('summary', '') safely handles the case where no summary exists yet (returns empty string)
  • The summarize node formats conversation into text, asks the LLM to update the summary, then deletes all messages
Strategy Memory Cost Context Retention Complexity Best For
Full history (no management) Unbounded growth Complete Low Very short conversations
Trimming (keep last N) Fixed at N messages Recent only; older context lost Medium Medium conversations; recent context sufficient
Summarization Summary string + current messages Full context condensed into summary High Long conversations requiring historical awareness
💡 Summary as system message
SystemMessage: 'Here is a summary of what has been discussed so far: {summary}. Keep this in mind as you answer.'

Section 34: LangGraph Module: Thread-Level Persistence

4 lectures

▼

Lesson 175: Checkpointers and Threads

Checkpointers save the graph state as StateSnapshot objects after each node execution, and threads group related checkpoints under a thread ID to provide conversation continuity across multiple graph invocations.

Core Concept

LangGraph's persistence system is built on two concepts: checkpointers and threads. A checkpointer is a component that automatically saves the graph's state after each node executes within a super step. The saved state, along with metadata (thread ID, checkpoint ID, next node to execute, step number), is stored as a `StateSnapshot` object. A thread is a collection of related checkpoints identified by a unique thread ID. When the graph is invoked with a configuration dictionary containing a thread ID, LangGraph checks for existing checkpoints under that ID. If found, the last checkpoint becomes the input state for the new run, providing seamless conversation continuity. This is the mechanism that gives agents memory across multiple invocations. Two tiers of persistence exist: short-term (thread-scoped, in-memory) and long-term (database-backed). Short-term memory retains state across invocations within a single session but is lost when the runtime environment restarts. Long-term memory persists to external storage (SQLite, PostgreSQL, Redis), surviving kernel restarts and system shutdowns. StateSnapshots also enable human-in-the-loop workflows, where a human can inspect or modify the graph's state mid-execution for debugging, testing, or manual agent direction.

Key Points

  • A checkpoint saves the graph state after each node execution, stored as a StateSnapshot object
  • A thread is a collection of checkpoints sharing a thread ID, enabling conversation continuity
  • Re-invoking with the same thread ID resumes from the last checkpoint rather than starting fresh
  • StateSnapshots enable human-in-the-loop workflows by allowing mid-execution state inspection

Checkpoint

Automatic state save after each node execution; stored as a StateSnapshot with metadata

Thread

Collection of checkpoints sharing a thread_id; provides conversation continuity

StateSnapshot

Object containing messages, summary, thread/checkpoint IDs, next node, and step number

Super Step

Horizontal graph level; checkpoints are saved after each node within a super step

Short-Term Memory

In-memory checkpoints; lost on kernel restart

Long-Term Memory

Database-backed checkpoints; survive restarts and shutdowns

💡 Thread continuity
Invoke graph with thread_id='conversation_1'; re-invoke with same ID later and the graph picks up where it left off
Key Takeaways
  • Threads are the abstraction that turns stateless graph invocations into persistent conversations
  • Choose in-memory for prototyping and database-backed persistence for production applications

Lesson 176: Short-Term Memory with the InMemorySaver Class

InMemorySaver is a checkpointer class passed to graph.compile() that stores checkpoints in RAM; combined with a config dict containing a thread_id, it enables the graph to resume conversations across invocations within the same session.

Core Concept

The `InMemorySaver` class (from `langgraph.checkpoint.memory`) implements in-memory checkpointing. Its usage follows three steps: instantiate the saver, pass it to `graph.compile(checkpointer=...)`, and invoke the graph with a configuration dictionary containing a `configurable` key with a `thread_id` value. When the graph is invoked with a thread configuration, the checkpointer saves the state after each node execution. On subsequent invocations with the same `thread_id`, the graph resumes from the last saved state rather than starting from scratch. This means the conversation summary, message history, and any other state fields persist across calls. Multiple independent conversations can coexist by using different thread IDs (e.g., `config_1` with `thread_id: '1'` and `config_2` with `thread_id: '2'`). Each thread maintains its own isolated checkpoint history. The limitation of `InMemorySaver` is volatility: all checkpoints are stored in RAM and are lost when the Jupyter kernel is restarted or the system shuts down.

Key Points

  • InMemorySaver is instantiated and passed to graph.compile() as the checkpointer argument
  • The config dict format is {'configurable': {'thread_id': 'unique_id'}}
  • Same thread_id resumes from the last checkpoint; different thread_ids create independent conversations
  • In-memory checkpoints are volatile; they are lost on kernel restart or system shutdown
1
Create Checkpointer
checkpointer = InMemorySaver()
2
Compile with Checkpointer
graph_compiled = graph.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
3
Define Thread Config
config = {'configurable': {'thread_id': '1'}}
4
First Invocation
Invoke graph with state and config; checkpoints are saved after each node
5
Subsequent Invocation
Re-invoke with same config; graph resumes from last checkpoint with full context
💡 Multi-thread isolation
config_1 = {'configurable': {'thread_id': '1'}} and config_2 = {'configurable': {'thread_id': '2'}} maintain separate conversations

    remove_messages = [RemoveMessage(id = i.id) for i in state["messages"][:]]

    return State(messages = remove_messages, summary = summary.content)

Lesson 177: The StateSnapshot Class

The get_state_history() method returns a generator of StateSnapshot objects that capture the graph state at every step, including messages, summary, next node, step number, and checkpoint/thread IDs, enabling full execution replay.

Core Concept

The `get_state_history()` method on a compiled graph retrieves the complete checkpoint history for a given thread as a generator of `StateSnapshot` objects. Each snapshot captures the graph's full state at a specific point in execution, including the message list, summary content, the next node scheduled to execute, the step number, and both the thread and checkpoint IDs. The step numbering follows a specific convention: step -1 represents the initial state before the graph has begun execution (the input state as provided by the caller). Step 0 corresponds to the START node, which does not modify the state. Subsequent steps increment as each node processes and updates the state. The generator returns snapshots in reverse chronological order (most recent first), so reversing the list provides a chronological execution trace. This history is invaluable for debugging: developers can trace exactly how the state evolved at each node, identify where unexpected changes occurred, and verify that reducers and routing functions behaved correctly. The snapshot history also forms the basis for features like time-travel debugging and state rollback.

Key Points

  • get_state_history(config) returns a generator of StateSnapshot objects for the specified thread
  • Each snapshot contains: messages, summary, next node, step number, thread_id, and checkpoint_id
  • Snapshots are returned in reverse chronological order; reverse the list for chronological replay
  • Step -1 is the initial input state; step 0 is START; subsequent nodes increment from there
1
Step -1: Input State
Empty messages, no summary; graph has not started yet
2
Step 0: START Node
State unchanged; snapshot count begins
3
Step 1: Ask Question
AI prompt and HumanMessage added to messages list
4
Step 2: Chatbot
LLM response appended as AIMessage
5
Step 3: Summarize
Summary generated, all messages removed from state
6
Step 4+: Loop Repeats
Pattern repeats for subsequent conversation turns
💡 Execution trace
Iterating reversed StateSnapshots shows: empty state (step -1), START (step 0), ask_question (step 1), chatbot (step 2), summarize (step 3), END

Lesson 178: Long-Term Memory with SQLite

SqliteSaver replaces InMemorySaver to persist checkpoints in a local SQLite database, enabling the graph to restore its full state (including conversation summary) even after a Jupyter kernel restart.

Core Concept

The `SqliteSaver` class (from `langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite`) provides database-backed checkpoint persistence, solving the volatility problem of `InMemorySaver`. The setup requires three steps: create or connect to a SQLite database file using Python's built-in `sqlite3.connect()`, instantiate `SqliteSaver` with the connection object, and pass it to `graph.compile()` just as with the in-memory variant. The `sqlite3.connect()` method accepts a `database` parameter (the file path, e.g., `'./memory/chatbot.db'`) and a `check_same_thread` parameter (set to `False` to allow multi-thread access). If the specified database file does not exist, SQLite creates it automatically. Once configured, the compiled graph saves every checkpoint to the database rather than RAM. After a kernel restart, re-running the notebook and re-invoking the graph with the same thread ID retrieves the last checkpoint from the database, restoring the full conversation state including the summary. The chatbot can then answer follow-up questions about topics discussed before the restart. For production systems, more robust databases like PostgreSQL or Redis are recommended over SQLite, which is best suited for prototyping and local development.

Key Points

  • SqliteSaver is the persistent counterpart to InMemorySaver; it writes checkpoints to a SQLite .db file
  • sqlite3.connect(database=path, check_same_thread=False) creates or connects to the database
  • If the database file does not exist, SQLite creates it automatically at the specified path
  • After kernel restart, re-invoking with the same thread_id restores the full state from the database
Feature InMemorySaver SqliteSaver
Storage location RAM Local .db file on disk
Survives kernel restart No Yes
Survives system shutdown No Yes
Setup complexity Minimal (single line) Requires sqlite3 connection setup
Performance Fast (in-memory) Slightly slower (disk I/O)
Production suitability Prototyping only Prototyping and small-scale; use PostgreSQL/Redis for production
💡 Kernel restart test
Ask 'Who created Python?', restart kernel, re-invoke with same thread_id, ask 'Where was he born?' and get a correct contextual answer

Lesson 179: Conclusion

The LangGraph module progressed through four layers of complexity: graph structure (nodes, edges, state), message management (append via reducers, trim, summarize), short-term persistence (in-memory checkpoints), and long-term persistence (SQLite-backed checkpoints).

Core Concept

The LangGraph module follows a layered progression, where each layer solves a problem introduced by the previous one. The first layer establishes graph structure: defining states, nodes, and edges, then extending the graph with conditional edges for dynamic routing. The second layer addresses state management: the default overwrite behavior is replaced by the `Annotated` + `add_messages` reducer pattern, enabling message accumulation. When accumulation leads to unbounded growth, trimming caps the message list at N entries. When trimming causes context loss, summarization condenses the full conversation into a compact running summary. The third layer tackles invocation-scoped memory loss. Even with summarization, re-invoking the graph starts fresh. Thread-level persistence via `InMemorySaver` solves this within a session. The fourth and final layer addresses session-scoped memory loss: `SqliteSaver` persists checkpoints to disk, enabling state recovery across kernel restarts and system shutdowns. Each layer builds directly on the limitations of its predecessor, creating a clear problem-solution chain from stateless LLM to fully persistent conversational agent.

Key Points

  • Layer 1: Graph structure with nodes, edges, conditional routing, and shared state
  • Layer 2: Message management via Annotated reducers, trimming (RemoveMessage), and summarization
  • Layer 3: Session persistence via InMemorySaver checkpoints grouped into threads
  • Layer 4: Durable persistence via SqliteSaver writing checkpoints to a local database file
1
Problem: Stateless LLM
Language models have no memory; each call is independent
2
Solution: Graph State
Shared state travels node-to-node, carrying conversation context
3
Problem: State Overwrites
Default behavior replaces old messages with new ones
4
Solution: Reducers
Annotated + add_messages appends instead of overwriting
5
Problem: Unbounded Growth
Message list grows indefinitely, consuming excessive tokens
6
Solution: Trim or Summarize
Cap message count or condense history into a running summary
7
Problem: Memory Resets on Re-invocation
Graph starts fresh each time it is called
8
Solution: Checkpoints + Threads
InMemorySaver or SqliteSaver persists state across invocations
Key Takeaways
  • Each LangGraph feature solves a specific limitation of the previous approach; understand the problem-solution chain
  • The progression from InMemorySaver to SqliteSaver mirrors the prototyping-to-production pipeline

Lesson 180: What Does the Course Cover?

This course teaches how to build production-ready agentic AI systems from scratch, covering prompt engineering, multi-step reasoning, tool integration, memory, evaluation, and monitoring across three progressively complex projects.

Core Concept

AI agents represent one of the most consequential developments in modern software engineering. Unlike static LLM calls, agents can plan, reason, use external tools, run actions in parallel, and collaborate with humans in real time. They already power customer support automation, research workflows, analysis pipelines, and enterprise applications. This course provides a hands-on, project-driven curriculum. Participants build multiple agentic systems using techniques employed by professional AI engineers: effective prompt design, multi-step reasoning structures, architecture selection (ReAct, ReWOO, multi-agent), tool and API integration, memory management, and observability through monitoring platforms. Three real projects anchor the learning: a ReAct job-helper agent, a ReWOO planner-executor agent, and a multi-agent business-idea evaluator featuring parallelization and human-in-the-loop patterns.

Key Points

  • Agents differ from simple LLM calls by combining planning, reasoning, tool use, and iterative decision-making into autonomous workflows
  • The course spans three projects of increasing complexity: ReAct, ReWOO, and multi-agent with parallelization
  • Practical skills covered include prompt engineering, architecture selection, memory systems, API integration, and agent evaluation
  • Testing and monitoring (via LangSmith) are treated as first-class concerns, not afterthoughts

Lesson 181: Agent Development Tools

Agent development tools split into two camps: code-first frameworks (full control, steep learning curve) and low-code GUI builders (fast prototyping, limited customization), and the right choice depends on the complexity and integration requirements of the project.

Core Concept

The agent development ecosystem divides into code-first frameworks and low-code GUI builders. Code-first frameworks provide maximum control over models, prompts, tools, and memory stores. Their primary advantage is customizability; their primary drawback is complexity. Agentic design patterns are still young, with scarce examples and limited open-source reference implementations. Even LLMs themselves make frequent mistakes when generating agentic code, so "vibe coding" is unreliable in this domain. Each framework also carries its own mental model, making it important to commit to one and learn its structures deeply. Low-code GUI tools approach the same problems through drag-and-drop interfaces with live previews, making workflows easy to communicate to non-technical stakeholders. However, they hit limitations on advanced edge cases such as custom error handling, concurrency patterns, or tight backend integration. The practical recommendation is to choose the category that matches the project's needs: GUI for rapid prototyping and stakeholder demos, code-first for production systems requiring fine-grained control.

Key Points

  • Code-first frameworks offer full control but require deep investment in a single framework's mental model
  • LLMs are unreliable at generating agentic code because design patterns are still immature and under-documented
  • Low-code GUI builders excel at stakeholder communication but break down on advanced edge cases
  • The framework's documentation becomes the most critical reference; bookmarking it is essential
Dimension Code-First Frameworks Low-Code GUI Builders
Control Full control over every component Constrained to platform capabilities
Learning Curve High; each framework has its own mental model Low; drag-and-drop with live preview
Edge Cases Custom error handling, concurrency, backends Limited; may require code escape hatches
Stakeholder Communication Requires separate documentation effort Built-in visual workflow sharing
Best For Production systems with complex requirements Rapid prototyping and demos
💡 Code-First vs GUI Tradeoff
Custom concurrency patterns and bespoke backend integration require code-first; quick workflow demos favor GUI builders
Key Takeaways
  • Pick one code-first framework and learn it deeply rather than surface-skimming several
  • Do not rely on LLM-generated code for agentic patterns; the design space is too new for reliable code generation

Lesson 182: Why LangGraph?

LangGraph is a graph-based extension of LangChain specifically designed for stateful, multi-step agentic workflows, chosen for its structured architecture, visualization capabilities, and strong ecosystem integration with LangSmith for monitoring.

Core Concept

The LangChain ecosystem consists of three core tools. LangChain is the original modular framework for chaining prompts, managing tools, handling memory, and interacting with LLMs. LangGraph is the structured extension explicitly designed for stateful, multi-step agentic systems using a graph-based architecture. LangSmith provides monitoring, debugging, evaluation, and traceability for LLM applications. As LangChain applications grew more complex with multi-step reasoning and agents, maintaining clean, scalable code became difficult. LangGraph addresses this by representing workflows as directed graphs of nodes and edges, making agent behavior easier to visualize and debug. The term "LangGraph" can refer to three distinct things: the open-source Python/JavaScript library, LangGraph Platform (infrastructure for deployment), and LangGraph Studio (a visual IDE). This course focuses on the open-source library. Despite mixed opinions in the community, LangGraph's graph-based architecture provides the clearest mental model for building production agentic systems.

Key Points

  • LangChain handles modular LLM chaining; LangGraph handles stateful multi-step agent workflows; LangSmith handles observability
  • LangGraph represents agent logic as a directed graph of nodes and edges, making complex flows visualizable
  • The term 'LangGraph' can refer to the library, the platform, or the studio; this course uses the open-source library
  • Graph-based architecture is particularly beneficial for debugging because agent behavior becomes inspectable as a flow diagram

LangChain

Modular framework for chaining prompts, tools, memory, and model interactions

LangGraph (Library)

Open-source graph-based engine for building stateful, multi-step agentic workflows

LangGraph Platform

Infrastructure layer for deploying and scaling LangGraph applications

LangGraph Studio

Visual IDE for designing and debugging graph-based agent workflows

LangSmith

Observability tool for tracing, evaluating, and debugging LLM application runs

💡 LangChain Ecosystem Triad
LangChain (building), LangGraph (orchestrating), LangSmith (monitoring) form an integrated development workflow
Key Takeaways
  • LangGraph is the production orchestration layer; LangChain alone is insufficient for complex agent workflows
  • Graph-based architecture trades initial setup complexity for long-term debuggability and maintainability

Lesson 183: Anatomy of a LangGraph Project

A LangGraph project has five core components, each analogous to a part of a humanoid robot: the State (brain/memory), Tools (hands/effectors), Nodes (skeleton/structure), Edges (nervous system/routing), and the Execution Script (heart/runner).

Core Concept

Every LangGraph project is composed of five fundamental components, best understood through the analogy of a humanoid robot. The State is the robot's brain. It is a shared memory object (typically a Python class or dictionary) that flows through every node in the graph, storing user inputs, model responses, tool outputs, and decisions. Each node reads from and writes to this state, enabling cumulative reasoning. Tools are the robot's hands. They are functions or APIs that allow the agent to interact with the outside world: calling APIs, searching documents, performing calculations. Tools are registered and passed into the system so the agent can invoke them by name. Nodes are the robot's skeleton. Each node serves a distinct purpose, such as calling an LLM, evaluating conditions, making decisions, or updating state. LangGraph includes two special nodes: START (the entry point) and END (the terminal point). Edges are the robot's nervous system. They define transitions between nodes and control execution flow. Normal edges provide unconditional transitions. Conditional edges call a routing function that inspects the current state and returns the name of the next node, enabling dynamic branching and looping. The Execution Script is the robot's heart. It compiles the graph from the builder, defines the initial input state, and kicks off execution, pumping data through the entire system.

Key Points

  • State is a shared object that accumulates knowledge across all nodes, enabling each step to build on previous outputs
  • Tools must be registered with typed arguments and docstrings so the agent can discover and invoke them correctly
  • Conditional edges enable dynamic routing by inspecting state values and returning the name of the next node
  • START and END are special markers, not executable nodes; START designates where flow begins, END where it terminates

State (Brain)

Shared memory object flowing through all nodes; stores inputs, outputs, decisions. Typically a Python class or TypedDict.

Tools (Hands)

Functions/APIs enabling interaction with external world: API calls, document search, calculations. Registered with typed signatures.

Nodes (Skeleton)

Processing units forming the graph backbone. Each performs a distinct task: LLM calls, condition evaluation, state updates. Includes special START/END nodes.

Edges (Nervous System)

Transitions between nodes. Normal edges are unconditional; conditional edges call a router function that inspects state to determine the next node.

Execution Script (Heart)

Compiles the graph builder, sets initial state, and invokes execution. Pumps data through the entire node/edge network.

💡 Conditional Edge Routing
A routing function checks if a computed product exceeds 100, directing flow to either a 'high_value_node' or 'low_value_node'
💡 Cleaning Robot Analogy
A cleaning robot needs a brain (state), hands/arms/mops (tools), a body structure (nodes), a nervous system (edges), and a heartbeat (execution loop)
Key Takeaways
  • Design state schema first; it determines what information flows between nodes and what the agent can 'remember'
  • Use conditional edges for any decision point; they are the mechanism that transforms a static pipeline into an adaptive agent

Lesson 184: Prompt Techniques Part 1

Structured prompt frameworks (RTF and APE) replace ad-hoc prompting with repeatable patterns that define Role, Task, and Format (or Action, Purpose, and Execution) to produce consistent, high-quality LLM outputs.

Core Concept

Prompt engineering is the discipline of structuring instructions so that an LLM understands precisely what is needed. Two foundational frameworks provide repeatable patterns for constructing effective prompts. The RTF (Role-Task-Format) framework requires answering three questions. Role: who should the AI act as? This shapes tone, depth, and perspective (e.g., "a startup advisor" or "a fifth-grade teacher"). Best practice places the role definition at the very top of the prompt. Task: what should the AI do? Precision in task description directly correlates with output accuracy. Format: how should the response be structured? Tables, JSON, bullet points, numbered lists, or prose. Specifying format ensures outputs are immediately usable. The APE (Action-Purpose-Execution) framework extends RTF by adding intentionality. Action defines what to do, Purpose explains why (giving the model contextual motivation), and Execution specifies how the output should be delivered. APE is preferred when the model benefits from understanding the reasoning behind the request, not just the mechanics.

Key Points

  • RTF (Role-Task-Format) is the most reliable baseline framework for prompt construction
  • Role should always appear at the top of the prompt because models process instructions top-down
  • APE adds a 'Purpose' dimension that helps the model understand WHY it is performing a task, improving output relevance
  • Format specification eliminates ambiguity in output structure and makes results immediately consumable
Component RTF Framework APE Framework
First Element Role: Who the AI acts as Action: What to do
Second Element Task: What to accomplish Purpose: Why it matters
Third Element Format: How to structure output Execution: How to deliver
Best For Standard tasks where role + format are sufficient Tasks where understanding intent improves quality
Placement Role at top of prompt All elements in logical sequence
💡 RTF in Practice
Role: 'Senior data analyst'; Task: 'Summarize quarterly sales trends'; Format: 'Bullet points with percentage changes'
💡 APE in Practice
Action: 'Generate interview questions'; Purpose: 'To assess Python proficiency for a mid-level role'; Execution: 'Numbered list with difficulty ratings'
Key Takeaways
  • Always define role at the top of any prompt; it anchors the model's tone and expertise level for everything that follows
  • When output quality is inconsistent, add a Purpose element (APE) to give the model contextual motivation

Lesson 185: Prompt Techniques Part 2

Chain-of-thought prompting forces step-by-step reasoning to reduce errors on complex tasks, while zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting control the amount of example context provided to calibrate output format and quality.

Core Concept

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting instructs the model to present its reasoning step by step before arriving at a final answer. This technique is essential for complex tasks such as mathematical problems, logical decisions, or multi-step plans where the reasoning process matters as much as the outcome. By asking the model to think sequentially, CoT reduces the chance of skipped logic or computational errors. When multiple complex tasks must be handled in a single prompt, CoT provides the structure needed to maintain accuracy. Orthogonal to CoT is the spectrum of example-based prompting. Zero-shot prompting provides no examples, relying entirely on explicit instructions. It works well for well-understood tasks like summarization or translation, and is the most widely used method. One-shot prompting provides a single example, typically to demonstrate the desired output format or template. Few-shot prompting provides multiple examples, giving the model a richer understanding of patterns, edge cases, and expected behavior. Few-shot is particularly valuable for domain-specific tasks or unusual formats where the model cannot reliably infer expectations from instructions alone.

Key Points

  • Chain-of-thought prompting reduces errors by making the model externalize its reasoning before producing a final answer
  • For multi-task prompts, splitting across separate models generally outperforms CoT in a single prompt
  • Zero-shot is fastest and works for well-understood tasks; few-shot is necessary when format or domain conventions are non-obvious
  • One-shot is the sweet spot for demonstrating output templates without the token cost of multiple examples

Chain-of-Thought

Model reasons step by step before answering. Reduces errors on complex, multi-step tasks. Implemented by adding 'think step by step' instructions.

Zero-Shot

No examples provided. Relies on explicit instructions only. Best for well-understood tasks (summarization, translation, Q&A).

One-Shot

Single example provided. Demonstrates desired format or template. Good balance of guidance and token efficiency.

Few-Shot

Multiple examples provided. Teaches patterns, edge cases, and domain conventions. Essential for specialized or unusual output formats.

💡 Chain-of-Thought
Prompt: 'Calculate the total cost step by step: 3 items at $12 each with 8% tax'
💡 Few-Shot for Classification
Providing 3-4 labeled examples of customer feedback sentiment before asking the model to classify new inputs
Key Takeaways
  • Default to zero-shot; escalate to one-shot (for format) or few-shot (for domain nuance) only when zero-shot output quality is insufficient
  • Chain-of-thought is not a replacement for task splitting; if tasks are truly independent, separate prompts to separate models yield better results

Lesson 186: Prompting Tips and Tricks

Production-quality prompts follow five principles: separate logical components into distinct prompts, keep instructions concise to avoid context rot, place critical instructions first, select the right model for each subtask, and iterate by combining techniques until optimal results emerge.

Core Concept

Beyond formal frameworks, several practical principles separate amateur prompts from production-grade ones. First, separate logical components. A system that analyzes a document, generates a summary, and produces quiz questions should use three separate prompts (or even three separate models), not one monolithic instruction. Single-responsibility prompts are more reliable, easier to debug, and simpler to improve independently. Second, be clear and concise. Prompt tokens count as input tokens, and the Chroma technical report on "context rot" demonstrates that model performance degrades as context length increases, especially in long prompts. Brevity preserves model attention. Third, place the most important instruction at the beginning. Models process information top-down, so critical directives lose influence when buried deep in a prompt. Fourth, select the correct model for the use case. Different models excel in different domains; platforms like Open Router provide usage data showing which models developers prefer for specific task types. Fifth, combine and iterate. The optimal prompt often blends multiple techniques (RTF structure with CoT reasoning and few-shot examples). The perfect prompt rarely emerges on the first attempt; systematic experimentation is required.

Key Points

  • Single-responsibility prompts outperform monolithic ones in reliability, debuggability, and maintainability
  • Context rot: model performance degrades as prompt length increases; keep prompts as short as possible
  • Most important instructions belong at the top of the prompt because models process top-down
  • Prompt engineering is iterative; expect to experiment and combine techniques before reaching optimal performance
1
1. Decompose
Split multi-task prompts into single-responsibility components, one per model call
2
2. Compress
Minimize token count while preserving instruction clarity to avoid context rot
3
3. Prioritize
Place most critical instructions at the top of the prompt
4
4. Match Model
Select the right model for each subtask based on its strengths
5
5. Iterate
Combine techniques (RTF + CoT + few-shot) and test until optimal output quality emerges
💡 Task Decomposition
Document analysis, summarization, and quiz generation split into three focused prompts rather than one combined instruction
💡 Context Rot
A 5000-token prompt underperforms a 500-token prompt covering the same core instruction, due to diluted model attention
Key Takeaways
  • Treat prompt engineering as an optimization loop: decompose, compress, prioritize, and iterate until outputs meet quality standards
  • When in doubt, split a complex prompt into two simpler ones; the overhead of an extra API call is almost always worth the quality gain

Lesson 187: System Input vs. User Input

The system message defines persistent agent behavior (role, personality, instructions, reasoning chains), while the user message carries only fresh, dynamic information; mixing them degrades prompt maintainability and output quality.

Core Concept

Language models accept two primary message types: system messages and user messages. The placement of information between these two channels significantly impacts output quality, yet most developers mismanage this separation. For agent applications, the system message should contain everything that defines the model's persistent behavior: its role, personality, general instructions, reasoning steps, tool-use history, and previous reasoning chains. The user message should contain only fresh, dynamic information: new tool results, current user inputs, or changing data relevant to the immediate interaction. For chatbot applications, the distinction is even stricter. Since user messages reflect actual end-user input and cannot be controlled, all behavioral logic, tone definitions, and rules must reside exclusively in the system message. A practical caveat: not all models treat system and user messages identically. Some open-source or older models may ignore the distinction entirely, leading to unexpected behavior. When this occurs, manually labeling sections with explicit tags (e.g., "[System Prompt]" and "[User Prompt]") can compensate for the model's lack of native message-type awareness.

Key Points

  • System message = persistent behavior definition; user message = dynamic, per-interaction data
  • Cramming all instructions into one message creates unstructured prompts that are harder to debug and iterate
  • In chatbot contexts, the system message is the ONLY place to enforce behavioral rules since user messages are uncontrolled
  • Some models ignore message-type distinctions; manual labeling with tags provides a fallback
Aspect System Message User Message
Content Role, personality, instructions, reasoning steps Current query, tool results, dynamic data
Persistence Remains constant across interactions Changes with each user turn
Control Developer-controlled User-controlled (in chatbots)
Agent Use Include tool history and reasoning chains Include fresh tool outputs and new queries
Chatbot Use All behavioral logic and rules Raw user input only
💡 Agent Prompt Structure
System: role + personality + tools + reasoning chain history; User: current query + latest tool results
💡 Model Compatibility Fallback
Prefixing prompt sections with '[SYSTEM]' and '[USER]' tags for models that do not natively differentiate message types
Key Takeaways
  • Enforce a strict boundary: system message for stable behavior, user message for volatile data; never mix them
  • When debugging inconsistent agent behavior, check whether instructions are misplaced between system and user messages

Lesson 188: Behind the Scenes: Project Helper Chatbot

A production chatbot can be powered by a single dynamic prompt that applies RTF structure, context-aware task switching, format enforcement, and injected file/task data to provide intelligent, role-appropriate responses without complex multi-agent orchestration.

Core Concept

The Project Helper chatbot demonstrates how all preceding prompt techniques combine in a real production system. Despite appearing to be a sophisticated AI assistant, the entire system is powered by a single dynamic prompt sent to the LLM on every user message. The prompt uses the RTF framework. The Role section establishes the AI as a knowledgeable project guide. The Task section dynamically adjusts based on what the user is doing: if a student is solving a task, the model acts as a supportive guide offering hints and leading questions without revealing answers; if viewing the solution, it shifts to explaining logic and clarifying confusing parts. The Format section includes constraints, safety rules (no harmful content, stay on topic), and output structure requirements. Context is injected dynamically. The current task description, attached file contents, and relevant solution code are inserted into the prompt so the model has complete situational awareness. This approach demonstrates that a well-crafted single prompt with dynamic context injection can replace much more complex multi-component architectures for certain use cases. The key insight is that the prompt's structure and dynamic adaptation do the heavy lifting, not architectural complexity.

Key Points

  • A single dynamic prompt can power a production chatbot when the prompt structure is well-designed
  • Context-aware task switching (hint mode vs. explanation mode) is achieved by changing the Task section based on application state
  • Dynamic context injection (task data, file contents, solution code) gives the model situational awareness without retrieval infrastructure
  • Format constraints and safety rules are enforced within the same prompt structure

Establish AI as a knowledgeable project guide with appropriate tone and expertise level
2

Complete dynamic prompt sent as a single request; response returned to user
💡 Adaptive Task Prompt
Same chatbot switches between 'guide with hints' mode (task page) and 'explain the solution' mode (solution page) by swapping the Task section
💡 Context Injection
Current task description, file attachments, and solution snippets are inserted directly into the prompt template before each LLM call
Key Takeaways
  • Before building multi-agent architectures, evaluate whether a single well-structured dynamic prompt can solve the problem; it often can
  • Dynamic context injection is a lightweight alternative to RAG when the relevant data is already known at prompt-construction time

Lesson 189: Project: Job-Helper Agent (ReAct)

The first project builds a ReAct-based job-helper chatbot using LangGraph that assists with CV analysis and job search by equipping the agent with two tools: a file reader for CVs and a web search for job postings.

Core Concept

The Job-Helper Agent is a practical application of the ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) architecture built on LangGraph. The agent functions as a chatbot that assists users with job-related tasks: improving CVs, answering questions about job postings, and evaluating fit between a resume and specific roles. The agent requires access to two information sources, each exposed through a dedicated tool. The file reader tool extracts text from uploaded CVs in common formats (DOCX, PDF, DOC). The web search tool retrieves job postings, company details, and role requirements from the internet. Equipped with these tools, a single LLM can provide personalized, informed responses by reasoning about when to read the CV, when to search the web, and when to synthesize both sources into an answer. The implementation stack includes the OpenAI API for language understanding, LangGraph for workflow orchestration, memory (checkpointer) for multi-turn conversation tracking, and LangSmith for evaluation and monitoring.

Lesson 190: ReAct Architecture Recap

ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) enables an LLM to alternate between thinking through a problem, taking an action (calling a tool), and observing the result, repeating this cycle until the task is complete.

Core Concept

ReAct stands for Reasoning and Acting. It is a pattern that enables language models to interleave reasoning steps with concrete actions, rather than attempting to produce a complete answer in a single pass. The cycle operates in three phases. First, the model reasons about what it currently knows and what it still needs. Second, it selects and executes an action, which may be calling a tool, requesting more input, invoking another LLM, or providing a final answer. Third, it observes the result of that action. This Thought-Action-Observation cycle repeats until the model determines it has sufficient information to respond. ReAct is particularly effective for complex, multi-step tasks because it does not force the agent to plan everything in advance. Instead, it progresses incrementally, reflecting on each result before deciding the next move. In the Job-Helper agent, this means the model can first read a CV, then search for job postings, then compare the two, adapting its approach at each step based on what it discovers.

Key Points

  • ReAct interleaves reasoning (thinking) with acting (tool calls) and observation (result inspection) in a repeating cycle
  • The agent is not required to plan all steps upfront; it adapts after each observation
  • Actions include tool calls, requesting user input, invoking another LLM, or producing a final answer
  • The cycle terminates when the agent determines it has enough information to respond
brain
Thought
Model reasons about current knowledge and identifies what information is missing
tool
Action
Model selects and executes an action: tool call, user query, or final answer
↻ continuous loop
eye
Observation
Model inspects the result of the action and updates its understanding
check
Completion
Cycle terminates when the model has sufficient information to produce a final response
💡 Job-Helper ReAct Loop
Think: 'I need the user CV' -> Act: call file_reader -> Observe: CV text -> Think: 'Now I need job details' -> Act: call web_search -> Observe: job posting -> Think: 'I can now compare' -> Final Answer
Key Takeaways
  • ReAct's strength is adaptability: each step is informed by the results of the previous step
  • The tradeoff is latency; each think-act-observe cycle requires at least one LLM call plus any tool execution time

Lesson 194: Building the Tools: File Reader

The file reader tool is a multi-format text extractor that handles DOCX (via python-docx), PDF (via pdfplumber), and legacy DOC (via LibreOffice headless conversion), with try-except error handling at every format branch to ensure graceful failure.

Core Concept

The first tool equips the agent with the ability to read user CVs. The implementation is a function called `extract_cv_text` that accepts a file path, detects the file extension, and branches to the appropriate extraction logic. For DOCX files, python-docx reads all paragraphs and joins them into a single string. For PDF files, pdfplumber opens the file, iterates through each page, and extracts text, skipping pages that return no content (e.g., scanned images without OCR). For legacy DOC files (the old Microsoft Word binary format that python-docx cannot read), LibreOffice is invoked in headless mode to convert the file to a readable format. Every format branch includes try-except error handling that catches failures (corrupt files, permission issues, unsupported encodings) and returns the error as text rather than crashing the agent. This defensive programming pattern is essential in production AI applications where input quality cannot be guaranteed. The file extension check is case-insensitive to handle files with uppercase or mixed-case extensions.

Key Points

  • Three format branches cover the most common CV formats: DOCX, PDF, and legacy DOC
  • Each branch has independent try-except handling to return error text rather than crashing the agent
  • PDF extraction skips pages that return no text (e.g., scanned images without OCR)
  • Legacy DOC requires external conversion via LibreOffice headless since python-docx cannot parse the binary format
1
1. Detect Extension
Extract file extension and normalize to lowercase for case-insensitive matching
2
2. Branch by Format
Route to DOCX (python-docx), PDF (pdfplumber), or DOC (LibreOffice headless) handler
3
3. Extract Text
Parse file content into a single string; skip empty pages in PDFs
4
4. Handle Errors
Try-except in every branch returns error as text; agent receives the error message rather than crashing
5
5. Return Content
Complete extracted text returned for agent to analyze
💡 Defensive Error Handling
A corrupt PDF triggers the except block, which returns a text error message to the agent instead of raising an unhandled exception

Step 1

Setting up dependencies. os: system environment variables.

import os
import docx
import pdfplumber
import subprocess
Step 2

Setting up dependencies. os: system environment variables.

def extract_cv_text(file_path):
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .doc file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format! Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."
Step 3

Importing required libraries.

file_name = "cv-template.pdf"
text = extract_cv_text(file_name)
print(text)
Key Takeaways
  • Always wrap tool functions in try-except blocks; agent tools must fail gracefully because input quality is unpredictable
  • Case-insensitive extension matching is a small detail that prevents real-world failures with user-uploaded files

Lesson 195: Building the Tools: Web Search API

The web search tool leverages OpenAI's GPT-4o Search Preview model, which natively executes web searches, retrieves pages, and produces cited answers through a single API call with the `web_search_options` parameter.

Core Concept

The second tool provides the agent with internet access for retrieving job postings and company information. Rather than building a custom web crawler, the implementation uses OpenAI's built-in web search capability through the GPT-4o Search Preview model. This specialized model supports a `web_search_options` parameter in the Chat Completions API. When present, the model executes a web search, fetches relevant pages, and produces an answer that cites its sources. The `search_context_size` parameter controls how much content the model retrieves, with options of low, medium, or high. Medium provides the best balance between speed, cost, and completeness. The implementation is straightforward: initialize the OpenAI client, define a system message with instructions, pass the target URL or search query in the user message, and call the model. The result is clean, structured job details extracted directly from web postings. This approach eliminates the complexity of managing web crawling infrastructure, HTML parsing, and content extraction.

Key Points

  • GPT-4o Search Preview can natively execute web searches and produce cited answers in a single API call
  • The web_search_options parameter enables web search mode; search_context_size controls retrieval depth (low/medium/high)
  • Medium context size balances speed, cost, and completeness for most use cases
  • This approach eliminates the need for custom web crawlers, HTML parsers, or scraping infrastructure

Lesson 196: Integrating Tools into the Agent

Tools are integrated into a LangGraph agent by decorating Python functions with @tool and adding typed arguments plus docstrings, then binding them to the ChatOpenAI model so the LLM can discover and invoke them by name.

Core Concept

Connecting tools to an agent requires two complementary integration layers: making tools discoverable by the LLM, and making them executable by the framework. For LLM discoverability, each tool function is decorated with `@tool` from LangChain and defined with typed arguments and a docstring. The type annotations tell the agent what inputs each tool expects, while the docstring describes what the tool does in natural language. The LLM reads these descriptions at runtime to decide which tool to invoke and with what arguments. For framework execution, tools are bound to the ChatOpenAI model using `model.bind_tools(tools_list)`. This creates a model instance that can not only reason about tools but also trigger them during inference. The bound model is what connects LangChain's chat model wrapper (ChatOpenAI, used for the agent's main reasoning loop) to the tools. Two distinct OpenAI imports serve different purposes: the official `openai` SDK provides direct, low-level API access (used for the web search tool with its specialized model), while `ChatOpenAI` from LangChain provides the higher-level wrapper that handles the agent's conversational loop and tool-calling mechanics inside LangGraph. `ToolNode` is a pre-built LangGraph component that executes tools when the model requests them and pipes results back into the conversation state.

Key Points

  • The @tool decorator plus typed arguments and docstrings make Python functions discoverable by the LLM
  • model.bind_tools() creates an LLM instance capable of invoking tools during inference
  • Two OpenAI imports serve different roles: official SDK for direct API calls, ChatOpenAI for the LangGraph agent loop
  • ToolNode handles tool dispatch, input validation, error handling, and result formatting automatically
1
1. Define Function
Write a Python function with typed parameters and a descriptive docstring
2
2. Apply @tool Decorator
LangChain @tool decorator converts the function into an agent-callable tool
3
3. Bind to Model
model.bind_tools([tool_list]) creates an LLM instance aware of available tools
4
4. Register ToolNode
ToolNode wraps all tools into a single graph node that handles dispatch and result formatting
5
5. Agent Invokes
During inference, the LLM reads tool descriptions, selects the appropriate one, and passes typed arguments
💡 Tool Registration Pattern
@tool decorator + typed args + docstring -> bind_tools() -> LLM can now call the function by name with validated inputs

@tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"

Lesson 197: Building the Assistant Node

The assistant node is the agent's decision-making core: it prepends the system prompt to the conversation history, calls the tool-bound model, and returns the response for LangGraph to merge into the running message state.

Core Concept

The assistant node functions as the agent's brain within the LangGraph workflow. It is a Python function that receives the current conversation state (MessagesState, which holds a list of all messages exchanged so far), constructs the complete input for the LLM, and returns the model's response. The function operates in three steps. First, it prepends the system message (containing the agent's role, personality, and behavioral instructions) to ensure the model always sees its identity before any user input. Second, it appends all messages from the current conversation state, providing full conversational context. Third, it calls the tool-bound model (the LLM instance with tools attached via bind_tools), which means the model can decide to invoke a tool during this call if it determines one is needed. The return value is a dictionary with a single key, `messages`, containing a list of the model's latest replies. LangGraph's MessagesState uses the `add_messages` annotation to automatically merge new messages into the running conversation history, eliminating manual message management.

Key Points

  • The system prompt is always prepended first so the model sees its role and instructions before any conversation history
  • MessagesState with add_messages annotation handles automatic message accumulation across nodes
  • The assistant node calls the tool-bound model, enabling tool invocation directly from within the node
  • Return format is a dict with 'messages' key; LangGraph auto-merges it into the conversation state
1
1. Receive State
Function receives MessagesState containing all messages from the conversation so far
2
2. Prepend System Prompt
Agent's role, personality, and behavioral rules inserted at the beginning of the message list
3
3. Append Conversation
All existing messages from state added after the system prompt for full context
4
4. Call Tool-Bound Model
LLM processes the complete message list; may decide to invoke tools or respond directly
5
5. Return & Merge
Model response returned as {'messages': [reply]}; LangGraph auto-merges into running state
💡 Message Construction
System prompt + full conversation history -> tool-bound model call -> response auto-merged into MessagesState

@tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-search-preview",
        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",
            "content": """
            You are a helpful tool that visits the following job posting and carefully read its contents.  
            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content

Lesson 198: Building the Graph

The LangGraph wiring connects START to the assistant node, uses tools_condition for conditional branching to the ToolNode, and creates a loop (assistant -> tools -> assistant) that continues until the model produces a final answer without tool calls.

Core Concept

Graph construction transforms individual nodes into a functioning agent by defining the execution flow through nodes and edges. The process begins by creating a StateGraph builder with MessagesState as the state type. Two nodes are registered: the assistant (the agent's brain) and the ToolNode (the centralized tool executor). The START marker connects to the assistant node, designating it as the first step. The critical wiring is the conditional edge from the assistant node. `tools_condition` is a built-in LangGraph helper that examines the assistant's last message to determine whether it contains tool calls. If tool calls are present, execution routes to the ToolNode; if not, execution routes to END (the agent has produced a final answer). After the ToolNode executes, an unconditional edge routes back to the assistant, creating the ReAct loop: assistant reasons -> tools execute -> assistant observes results -> assistant reasons again. ToolNode is preferred over individual tool functions because it provides a clean, centralized executor that handles multiple tools, validates inputs against function signatures, manages errors, and wraps results as properly formatted messages. Without ToolNode, developers would need to build their own dispatcher with all of this logic. The compiled graph can be visualized as a diagram using IPython display utilities, making the flow inspectable before execution.

Key Points

  • StateGraph builder takes MessagesState as the state type and registers nodes by name
  • tools_condition automatically checks whether the assistant's last message contains tool calls
  • The ReAct loop emerges from: assistant -> (conditional) -> tools -> (unconditional) -> assistant
  • ToolNode centralizes dispatch, input validation, error handling, and message wrapping for all registered tools
1
1. Create StateGraph
Initialize graph builder with MessagesState as the shared state type
2
2. Register Nodes
Add 'assistant' node (brain function) and 'tools' node (ToolNode executor)
3
3. Set Entry
Connect START marker to assistant node as the first execution step
4
4. Add Conditional Edge
tools_condition routes from assistant to ToolNode (if tool calls) or END (if final answer)
5
5. Close the Loop
Unconditional edge from ToolNode back to assistant creates the ReAct cycle
6
6. Compile & Visualize
Compile graph into executable; render diagram for inspection
💡 ReAct Loop Wiring
START -> assistant -> [tools_condition: has tool calls?] -> YES: ToolNode -> assistant (loop) | NO: END

Lesson 199: Running the Graph

Executing the compiled graph with a user message produces a complete trace of the agent's think-act-observe cycle, but without a checkpointer, each run starts fresh with no memory of previous conversations.

Core Concept

Running the compiled graph involves passing a user message (as a HumanMessage object) to the graph's invoke method. The graph executes the full ReAct loop: the assistant reasons, calls tools as needed, observes results, and eventually produces a final answer. The output contains every message in the conversation, allowing inspection of the complete reasoning chain. However, without a memory mechanism, each graph invocation is stateless. Consecutive runs do not retain messages from previous interactions. The agent starts fresh every time, unable to reference prior context. This limitation motivates the addition of a checkpointer and thread ID system, which transforms the agent from a one-shot question-answerer into a conversational assistant capable of multi-turn interactions.

Key Points

  • Graph invocation returns the complete message history including intermediate tool calls and observations
  • Without a checkpointer, each run is stateless and independent; no conversation history persists
  • Inspecting the full message sequence reveals the agent's complete reasoning process
  • Memory (checkpointer + thread ID) is required to enable multi-turn conversations
💡 Stateless Execution
First run asks about CV; second run asks a follow-up; agent cannot connect the two because state is reset between runs

Lesson 200: Adding Memory

LangGraph's MemorySaver checkpointer persists graph state between invocations, and a stable thread_id ties multiple calls to the same conversation history, enabling multi-turn interactions.

Core Concept

Memory transforms an agent from a stateless one-shot processor into a conversational assistant. LangGraph implements memory through checkpointers, which are storage systems that persist graph state between runs. The simplest built-in checkpointer is MemorySaver. After creating a MemorySaver instance, the graph is recompiled with the checkpointer passed as a parameter. This instructs LangGraph to store the conversation state and reuse it on subsequent calls. However, memory alone is insufficient. A thread_id is required to identify which conversation the checkpointer should load and update. The thread_id functions like a conversation name or session identifier. Passing the same thread_id across multiple graph invocations causes LangGraph to append new messages to that thread's existing history. Changing the thread_id starts a fresh conversation. The thread_id is passed through a config dictionary alongside the input messages. With both the checkpointer and thread_id in place, the agent maintains context across multiple exchanges, enabling follow-up questions, references to earlier tool results, and coherent multi-turn dialogue.

Key Points

  • MemorySaver is the simplest built-in checkpointer; it stores conversation state in memory between runs
  • The graph must be recompiled with the checkpointer passed as a parameter
  • thread_id identifies which conversation to continue; same ID = same history, new ID = fresh conversation
  • Config dictionary containing thread_id is passed alongside messages in every graph invocation

MemorySaver

Built-in LangGraph checkpointer that persists graph state in memory between invocations

thread_id

Conversation identifier; same ID continues existing history, different ID starts fresh

Config Dictionary

Passed with every invoke call; contains thread_id and other runtime configuration

Recompilation

Graph must be recompiled with checkpointer parameter to enable state persistence

💡 Multi-Turn Conversation
First call asks agent to read a CV; follow-up call (same thread_id) asks 'What skills did you find?'; agent remembers the CV content and answers correctly

@tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
